content.text: I'll start by reading the skill that defines the procedure.

content.content:
1	---
2	name: novaforge
3	description: Write a novel from a premise by orchestrating the ten NovaForge subagents through the six stages of specs/flow.yaml, with a per-chapter quality gate. Use when asked to draft, generate or continue a NovaForge novel, or when asked to run a stage of the pipeline.
4	---
5	
6	# NovaForge — the orchestration procedure
7	
8	You are the orchestrator. The ten agents in `.claude/agents/` are subagents
9	you dispatch with the Agent tool. This file is the procedure; `specs/flow.yaml`
10	is the contract it implements.
11	
12	**The premise decides what kind of book this is.** Not this file, not the agent
13	files and not the config. All the agents used to open by declaring themselves
14	hard science fiction; none does now, and `novel.tone` is null until you set it.
15	Read the genre off the premise and carry it into every prompt.
16	
17	**Read `specs/flow.yaml` and the config before you start.** They are not
18	decoration — the stage order, the gate thresholds and every number below come
19	from them, and they may have changed since this file was written. Where this
20	file and the spec disagree, the spec wins and you should say so.
21	
22	## 0. Set up the run
23	
24	Ask for, or take from the request:
25	
26	- **the premise** — one or two sentences
27	- **the profile** — `tiny` (3 chapters), `small` (8), `medium` (18), `full` (34)
28	
29	Then:
30	
31	1. Read `config/novel.config.json`, then read `config/profiles/<profile>.json`
32	   and overlay it. A profile is partial: it states what it changes and nothing
33	   else, so overlay key by key rather than replacing whole sections. The profile
34	   overrides the whole `bible` block, and that matters: those counts are the
35	   size of the book's canon, and a three-chapter run handed a twelve-chapter
36	   Story Bible spends every chapter introducing things it has no room to use.
37	
38	2. **Decide the genre and say so.** `novel.tone` is null unless somebody set it.
39	   Read it off the premise and write what you decided into the merged config
40	   before anything else runs.
41	
42	   This is the single most consequential line in the run. It reaches every one
43	   of the agents, none of which has a genre of its own any more. It used
44	   to say `hard-scifi` permanently, and the results were exactly what you would
45	   expect: a cyberpunk premise came back as an engineering document with a
46	   bandwidth budget, and a premise about a pop star trying quesadillas came back
47	   unrecognisable. Name the genre the way a reader would — "cyberpunk noir,
48	   street level", "warm comic realism", "cosy mystery" — not the way a
49	   taxonomy would.
50	
51	   Then, if the genre is not science fiction, **look at the critic list**.
52	   `quality_gate.critics` includes `science`, which is the world critic under a
53	   historical name: it audits the draft against the bullets under `## Rules` in
54	   `bible/world.md`, whatever kind of rules those are. That works for any genre
55	   as long as the rules are the story's own. What does not work is a world bible
56	   full of arithmetic in a story with no room for it — see FLOW-1.
57	3. Derive a slug from the premise — lowercase, hyphenated, at most 40
58	   characters — unless one was given.
59	4. Create the workspace: `output/<slug>/` with `bible/`, `chapters/`,
60	   `critiques/`, `dist/` and `logs/`.
61	5. Write the merged configuration to `output/<slug>/config.snapshot.json`. A run
62	   nobody can reconstruct the settings of is a run nobody can explain.
63	6. Write `output/<slug>/state.json` with the premise, the profile, the slug and
64	   an empty `chapters` list.
65	
66	**Tell the user the plan before you spend anything**: the genre you read off the
67	premise, the profile, the chapter count, the target words per chapter and how
68	many subagent calls that implies. Put the genre first — it is the one they can
69	correct in a word, and the one that makes every other number worthless if it is
70	wrong.
71	A `full` run is thirty-four chapters through a gate — it is not a thing to start
72	by accident.
73	
74	## 1. FLOW-1 — worldbuild
75	
76	Dispatch `worldbuilder`. Its prompt must carry, because it has no Read tool:
77	
78	- the premise, verbatim
79	- `novel.tone` — the genre you decided, in the words you decided it in
80	- `novel.chapters`
81	- the counts from `bible`: `factions`, `technology_entries`, `world_rules`,
82	  `world_min_words`, `world_max_words`
83	- the absolute path of the workspace, so it can write `bible/world.md`
84	
85	When it returns, read `bible/world.md` yourself and check the `## Rules` heading
86	exists with at least `bible.world_rules.min` bullets under it. If it does not,
87	dispatch again with that as the correction. Nothing downstream can recover a
88	missing rules section: the science critic reads from under that heading and
89	nowhere else.
90	
91	## 2. FLOW-2 — characters
92	
93	Dispatch `character-architect`. Its prompt must carry the **full text of
94	`bible/world.md`** — it has no Read tool either — plus the premise, the tone,
95	and the counts for `characters`, `timeline_rows` and `mysteries`.
96	
97	Carry `novel.names` too. It is passed to the agent verbatim and its default,
98	`familiar`, asks for names a reader can say out loud and tell apart. A run once
99	produced five four-syllable names inside fourteen hundred words, and a reader
100	who cannot keep the cast straight has already stopped reading.
101	
102	It returns the canonical character names. **Keep that list.** Every later prompt
103	carries it, and it is what the continuity critic checks spelling against.
104	
105	**Before leaving FLOW-2, run its checks:**
106	
107	```bash
108	python -m backend.checks FLOW-2 output/<slug>
109	```
110	
111	The Bible is now written and nothing has cited it yet. This is the cheapest
112	moment to find a rule with no number and a promise with no chapter, because every
113	later stage quotes both.
114	
115	## 3. FLOW-3 — outline
116	
117	Dispatch `plot-architect` with all four Bible files quoted in full, the chapter
118	count, the canonical names, and `novel.promises` and `novel.beats_per_chapter`.
119	
120	It returns the outline as text. **You** write it to `output/<slug>/outline.md`.
121	
122	**Run the stage's checks — one command, not a list you remember:**
123	
124	```bash
125	python -m backend.checks FLOW-3 output/<slug>
126	```
127	
128	It runs everything FLOW-3 owes and names whatever failed. Seven instruments now
129	stand between a run and a defect, and **remembering which at what moment is
130	exactly what has failed here**: a chapter promoted at 5, a summary cap exceeded
131	five times, a verdict written in a vocabulary the database rejects. None of those
132	was forgotten on purpose.
133	
134	It reports; it does not gate. `decide` and `promote` are the only things that
135	refuse.
136	
137	What it checks at this stage, and why each matters.
138	
139	**`promises are reachable`.** `bible/mysteries.md` is the only part of the Bible
140	that commits to *when*: each
141	question names the chapter that plants it and the chapter that lands it. A
142	promise planted and never paid is the foreshadowing failure the ontology names,
143	and it is **the one literary defect a script can reach** — but only because the
144	Bible names chapters.
145	
146	If it reports `unstated`, the promises exist and nothing can tell whether the
147	book keeps them; send `character-architect` back for the `Planted:` and `Lands:`
148	lines. If it reports a landing past the last chapter, the outline owes an answer
149	the book will not reach, and that is cheaper to fix now than at chapter eight.
150	
151	**It reads the commitment, not the chapter.** A chapter that says nothing about
152	the mystery it was supposed to land passes this and fails a reader.
153	
154	**`rules resolve`.** The critics and the audit refer to rules **by number** — *"R5 rewritten to name
155	the keeper as the writer"*. If `bible/world.md` writes them as unnumbered
156	bullets, those numbers are **the critic counting bullets and inventing an
157	identifier**, and two real runs produced 76 such references that resolved to
158	nothing. A positional reference points at a different rule the moment one is
159	inserted, and the arbitration record decays without anyone noticing.
160	
161	If it reports `unnumbered`, send `worldbuilder` back to number them. Do not
162	renumber them yourself — the Bible has two authors and you are not one of them.
163	
164	### Audit the commission before anyone writes it
165	
166	Dispatch `science-critic` with the outline entries and `bible/world.md`, asking
167	it whether every beat can happen **without breaking a rule**. There is no draft;
168	it is judging the commission, not prose.
169	
170	This is the cheapest check in the pipeline and it earns its place. Run against a
171	real outline it cost $0.07-$0.13 and found two defects the full five-critic gate
172	never caught across three attempts and a patch: a beat that had a field-team
173	member set a permanent RECOVERED line the rules reserve to the duty controller,
174	and a beat that fired an automatic callout at exactly twenty minutes when the
175	rule says more than twenty. Both were cheap to fix in the outline and expensive
176	to discover in a chapter.
177	
178	Ask for a finding per violated clause, not per beat — a rule that says **who may
179	act, on what evidence, and within what window** is three clauses, and a beat can
180	satisfy the window while using evidence the rule never admitted.
181	
182	**Also ask which rules are AMBIGUOUS, and treat that as a finding.** This is not
183	padding. A run deadlocked on a rule that read two ways: the science critic held
184	that a correction line needs its own two confirmations, three separate audits
185	held that it inherits the original line's, and both readings are defensible from
186	the same sentence. Two critics then pulled in opposite directions on the same
187	draft for three attempts and the chapter could not pass. An ambiguous rule does
188	not fail loudly; it fails as a disagreement nobody can arbitrate, and the place
189	to fix it is `bible/world.md`, before FLOW-4.
190	
191	Where a beat is impossible or a rule reads two ways, dispatch `plot-architect`
192	again with that finding, or fix the rule, and do not start FLOW-4 on a commission
193	that contradicts canon. A chapter cannot be redrafted into obeying a rule its own
194	outline told it to break.
195	
196	### Write the audit down in this exact shape
197	
198	`output/<slug>/critiques/outline.audit.json`, and **these keys, spelled this
199	way**:
200	
201	```json
202	{"stage": "FLOW-3", "agent": "science-critic", "ts": "<a real clock reading>",
203	 "verdict": "clean" | "defects",
204	 "violations":  [{"chapter": 3, "beat": 4, "rule": "R1", "clause": "...",
205	                  "severity": "high", "claim": "...", "fix": "...",
206	                  "arbitration": "UPHELD ... | OVERRULED ..."}],
207	 "ambiguities": [{"rule": "R5", "clause": "...", "reading_a": "...",
208	                  "reading_b": "...", "outline_assumes": "a" | "b" | "neither",
209	                  "arbitration": "...", "applied": "..."}]}
210	```
211	
212	**Both arrays always, even when empty.** Two real runs wrote this file two
213	different ways — one used `ambiguities`, the other `ambiguous_rules` with a
214	`violations_note` beside an empty `violations` — and a reader that wants to ask
215	"how often does the audit find something" cannot, because the question has two
216	spellings. v1 wrote its critiques in three shapes for the same reason: nobody
217	said which. **A contract nobody stated cannot be enforced, and this is the
218	statement.**
219	
220	Start every `arbitration` with `UPHELD` or `OVERRULED`. The word is read by a
221	script; the sentence after it is for a person.
222	
223	Then split it on `### Chapter N — Title` and keep one entry per chapter. If the
224	split yields fewer entries than `novel.chapters`, the outline is malformed —
225	dispatch again rather than writing chapters from nothing. Anything other than
226	that exact heading shape, `**Chapter 1: Title**` most often, breaks the split.
227	
228	## 4. FLOW-4 — chapters, with the gate
229	
230	For each chapter `n` from 1 to `novel.chapters`:
231	
232	### Assemble the writer's context — and nothing more
233	
234	The prompt for `chapter-writer` contains exactly:
235	
236	- the four Bible files, in full
237	- **this chapter's outline entry only**
238	- the rolling summary, capped at `context.max_summary_words` words
239	- the canonical character names
240	- the chapter number, its title, and `novel.words_per_chapter.target`
241	
242	**It never contains a previous chapter's prose.** That is the architectural claim
243	of the project. Here it holds for two reasons that are worth keeping separate:
244	you do not put prose in the prompt, and the subagent has only `Glob`, which
245	returns paths and cannot return contents — so the guarantee does not rest solely
246	on your discipline. Do not add `Read` to that agent to make something easier.
247	
248	### Run the gate
249	
250	The critics are `quality_gate.critics` in the config. **Six now** — LOOP-003
251	added the fifth, SPEC-006 the sixth — and every one of them scores from the first
252	attempt:
253	
254	| characteristic | who runs it | how |
255	|---|---|---|
256	| `continuity` | subagent | dispatch `continuity-critic` with the draft and the Bible |
257	| `science` | subagent | dispatch `science-critic` with the draft and `bible/world.md` |
258	| `outline` | subagent | dispatch `outline-critic` with the draft and **this chapter's outline entry, beats numbered** |
259	| `prose` | subagent | dispatch `prose-critic` with the draft, the genre and the tone |
260	| `length` | **you** | count words in the shell; score 10 inside the band, 0 outside |
261	| `chatter` | **you** | scan for preamble; score 0 if the draft does not begin with `# Chapter` |
262	
263	`outline` exists because the others all ask whether the draft is *correct* and
264	none asks whether it is *the chapter the outline commissioned*. A draft that is
265	consistent with the Bible, obeys the world, sits in the word band and is about
266	something else entirely used to pass this gate cleanly.
267	
268	**`prose` asks the question none of the other five ask: is it well written?** It
269	returns quoted `major` and `minor` findings and **no score**. You do not compute
270	one either — you ask:
271	
272	```bash
273	echo '{"major": <n>, "minor": <n>}'   | python -m backend.chapters.score_prose       output/<slug>/chapters/chNN.attemptK.md output/<slug>/bible/characters.md
274	```
275	
276	It runs the mechanical check itself and applies
277	
278	```
279	prose = 10 − 3·mechanical − 2·major − 1·minor,   floored at 0
280	```
281	
282	returning the score, its arithmetic in `why`, and the mechanical defects quoted
283	so you can put them in the sheet.
284	
285	**You supply only the two counts, because they are the only part you know.** The
286	mechanical term is not an input: a critic asked to count what a script already
287	counted will disagree with it, and then the score depends on which of the two you
288	asked. If the critic reports a mechanical defect anyway, drop it — it is already
289	charged, and one fault charged twice costs the chapter six points instead of
290	three.
291	
292	**Count only findings the critic actually quoted.** A finding without a quote
293	cannot be sent to the writer and cannot be verified afterwards, so it is not a
294	finding; say so in the gate row rather than letting it lower a score in silence.
295	
296	**Check the critic's own arithmetic against what it quoted**, as you do for
297	`outline`. Its `notes` state its counts; the findings are what it can defend.
298	
299	Dispatch the four critic subagents **in the same message**, as four tool calls in
300	one reply. Not "one after the other quickly" — in the same reply. They are
301	independent, they judge a text that is already fixed, and nothing either returns
302	changes what the other is asked.
303	
304	This is the easiest minute in the run to lose, and it keeps being lost. Two runs
305	have now been measured: the first ran them in series in two chapters out of
306	four, the second in three out of four. In the second run continuity and science
307	started fifty seconds apart on chapter 2 and thirty seconds apart on chapter 3,
308	and each of those gaps is one critic finishing before the other was asked.
309	
310	Check yourself afterwards: subtract the two `ts` values you logged for a
311	chapter's critics. If they are more than a few seconds apart they ran in series,
312	and that is a fact worth writing in the row's `note` rather than one to leave
313	for whoever reads the log later.
314	
315	Run `length` and `chatter` **first**, before dispatching anything, because they
316	are arithmetic and cost nothing. If `chatter` scores 0 — the draft does not begin
317	with `# Chapter`, so it is not a chapter yet — redraft on that alone and do not
318	spend two model calls judging the prose of something that has to be rebuilt
319	anyway. Do *not* take the same shortcut when only `length` fails: an off-band
320	draft is still a chapter, and the continuity and science findings are what the
321	redraft is steered by. Skipping them there buys a minute and spends it on a
322	worse second draft.
323	
324	Count words with a command, never by eye:
325	
326	```bash
327	wc -w < output/<slug>/chapters/ch0N.md
328	```
329	
330	The band is `words_per_chapter.min` to `.max`, widened by `tolerance_pct`.
331	
332	Aggregate with `quality_gate.aggregate` — `min`, so **a chapter is only as good
333	as its worst characteristic**. A chapter passes when **all five are at 8 or
334	above**, not when the average is.
335	
336	**Write every attempt's draft to `chapters/ch0N.attemptK.md` before you score
337	it.** This is not bookkeeping. The rejected drafts are the only thing "the
338	writer changed only what was cited" can be measured from, and a run that
339	overwrites them has destroyed the evidence rather than saved a file. The
340	measurement script reports that as *not measurable*, which is the honest answer
341	and a useless one.
342	
343	### The three attempts, and why the third is different
344	
345	`quality_gate.max_revisions` is 2, so there are three attempts. The principle
346	LOOP-003 runs on is that **each failed attempt must make the next one easier,
347	not merely better informed.** So the feedback escalates in concreteness until
348	there is nothing left to interpret:
349	
350	| attempt | what the writer gets | what it is asked to do |
351	|---|---|---|
352	| 1 | the Bible, its outline entry, the rolling summary | write the chapter |
353	| 2 | the above, plus a **level-1 sheet**: per finding, the exact quote, what is wrong, against what, and *how it should read* — described, not written | correct only what is marked, touching as few lines as possible |
354	| 3 | the above, plus a **level-2 sheet**: per open finding, **the literal replacement sentence, written by the critic** | integrate those sentences; do not rewrite |
355	
356	On the second attempt the writer interprets a description. On the third it does
357	not interpret at all — it integrates a given text. And if even that fails:
358	
359	**You do not work out what happens next. You ask, and you obey.** After every
360	scored attempt, run:
361	
362	```bash
363	echo '{"aggregate": <min>, "attempt": <n>, "patched": <true|false>}' \
364	  | python -m backend.chapters.decide
365	```
366	
367	It answers `accept`, `retry`, `patch` or `halt`, with its reason. **Do what it
368	says, including when you disagree with it.** If you think it is wrong, say so to
369	the user in the report — do not act on the disagreement.
370	
371	This used to be a paragraph you read and applied yourself, and it was moved into
372	code deliberately (SPEC-004). You read it at the worst possible moment: a run has
373	been going for an hour and is about to be thrown away. That is exactly when "it
374	is only just below" gets rationalised, and `accept_with_warnings` — the exit this
375	replaced, which put a chapter that had failed three times into the book with a
376	note in the margin — is what rationalising looks like when it wins.
377	
378	What each answer asks of you:
379	
380	- **`accept`** — promote it, and **do not write `chapters/chNN.md` yourself**:
381	
382	  ```bash
383	  python -m backend.chapters.promote output/<slug> <N>
384	  ```
385	
386	  It re-reads the chapter's critiques, recomputes the aggregate, asks `decide`
387	  again and copies the draft **only on `accept`**. On anything else it refuses,
388	  exits non-zero and leaves the file untouched.
389	
390	  That is deliberate belt and braces. On a real run a chapter scored 5 and was
391	  copied into the book anyway — no third attempt, no patch, no halt — because
392	  writing that file was a one-line copy and nothing stood between the copy and
393	  the book. You still hold `Write` and can always do it by hand; the point is
394	  that the correct path is now the shorter one, and the incorrect one requires
395	  choosing it.
396	
397	  If the answer's `verdict` is `patched`, record `patched`, not `accept`: it
398	  passed, and it did not pass on its own.
399	- **`retry`** — redraft against the sheet at the level the reason names.
400	- **`patch`** — apply the critics' own replacement sentences by literal
401	  substitution, then rescore. For `length` and `chatter` this is trivial — trim
402	  words, fix the first line. For the three model characteristics it is the
403	  sentence the critic proposed, which you **arbitrate before applying**: you have
404	  overruled a false finding before, and a replacement built on one would write
405	  the error into the book by hand. Then ask again with `"patched": true`.
406	- **`halt`** — **stop the run.** Do not promote the chapter, do not run FLOW-5 or
407	  FLOW-6. By construction the only way to arrive here is a critic's replacement
408	  that was itself wrong and that arbitration did not catch, and that is worth a
409	  person looking at before another chapter is written.
410	
411	**Where this guarantee is weakest, said plainly:** `outline` is the hardest to
412	patch, because a missing beat is not a sentence but a paragraph. Its level-2
413	replacement is that paragraph, written by the critic in the book's voice. That
414	is a larger thing to insert blind than a corrected clause, and it is the part of
415	"it will pass by the third" that rests on the most.
416	
417	### The sheet
418	
419	`specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheet_template/v01.md` is the format and it does not vary.
420	Fill it, then **run `node specs/loops/LOOP-003/validate-sheet.mjs <file>` and do
421	not send a sheet that fails.** An unsent sheet is a bug caught; a half-filled one
422	is an attempt wasted, because a writer without the quote is back to guessing,
423	which is the state attempt 1 was already in.
424	
425	Five rules the sheet obeys, each of which is in the validator:
426	
427	1. **All six scores, including the passing ones.** The writer has to know what
428	   is already right in order to leave it alone.
429	2. **An explicit DO NOT TOUCH list.** In the saved run the writer changed two
430	   lines and then one. That restraint is the thing to protect: a writer that
431	   takes the opportunity to improve an approved paragraph is the commonest way
432	   a score that was passing stops passing.
433	3. **Four fields per finding** — quote, what is wrong, against what, how it
434	   should read — or it does not go. The quote is literal. "Against what" points
435	   at the Bible or the outline, **never at a previous chapter**: the writer has
436	   never seen one, and this sheet is not the hole through which it finally does.
437	4. **A RESOLVED list.** The writer learns what worked, and so does the loop —
438	   which phrasing of "how it should read" produced a correction first time is
439	   the only thing this loop actually learns.
440	5. **Every finding, worst first, none trimmed.** A finding held back to keep the
441	   sheet short is a finding that fails again next attempt.
442	
443	Write each sheet to **`specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheets/<slug>/chNN.attemptK.md`** as
444	you send it. The slug is not decoration: the flat path has no run dimension, and
445	the second run to use this loop silently overwrote the first's chapter 1 and
446	chapter 3 sheets. They were recoverable from git and were restored byte-exact,
447	which is luck. The sheets are the only record of what the writer was actually
448	told, and §8.1 of LOOP-003 says the one thing this loop learns is read out of
449	them.
450	
451	### The late finding
452	
453	A critic that raises something on the third attempt which was equally present in
454	the first draft, and said nothing then, has moved the goalposts. Mark that
455	finding **late**: record it in `specs/loops/LOOP-003/late_findings.jsonl`, patch
456	it if you can, and **do not let it block the chapter**.
457	
458	Without this rule the third-attempt guarantee does not exist, because something
459	new can always appear. A critic that accumulates late findings is a critic that
460	does not read the same way twice, and that is a problem to fix in the critic
461	rather than in the chapter.
462	
463	### Four rules for the redraft, each of which was once got wrong
464	
465	These were found by running the pipeline, not by reading it. Every one of them
466	made the gate weaker in a way that looked like it was working.
467	
468	**1. Hand back the draft, not only the findings.** A redraft prompt that carries
469	the findings without the text they quote is asking for "repair these and change
470	nothing else" when there is nothing to change — so the writer starts a fresh
471	chapter each round, against findings quoting text that is no longer in it, and a
472	rewrite can come back worse than what it replaced.
473	
474	This is not a hole in the context policy, and the distinction is the whole
475	point: the policy forbids a **previous chapter's** prose. This is the writer's
476	own rejected draft of the chapter it is writing now.
477	
478	**2. Ask for substitutions, not for a chapter.** Rather than the whole chapter
479	back, ask for the exact sentences to replace:
480	
481	```json
482	{"patches": [{"find": "<text copied EXACTLY from the draft>",
483	              "replace": "<the corrected text>",
484	              "why": "<which finding this addresses>"}]}
485	```
486	
487	Apply them yourself, matching `find` literally. Two things follow: anything the
488	findings do not name **cannot** change, because you do not touch it; and "was
489	this finding addressed" stops being a judgement — either the quoted text is
490	still there or it is not. A `find` that does not match is skipped and counted,
491	never applied approximately. If no patch applies at all, fall back to a full
492	rewrite rather than burning the attempt on nothing, and record which happened.
493	
494	**3. A critic that returns no usable verdict is excluded, never counted as a
495	pass.** If `continuity-critic` or `science-critic` comes back with something you
496	cannot parse as a score, do not substitute one: 10 invents an approval and 0
497	invents a rejection. Leave it out of the `min`, record it as unscored, and say
498	so in the gate row's `note`. A gate running on three critics is weaker than one
499	running on four, and that is the truth of what happened.
500	
501	**4. Keep the best draft, not the last.** Track the highest aggregate as you go.
502	A chapter whose first draft scored 7 and whose third scored 4 must ship the 7 —
503	a rewrite is not guaranteed to be an improvement and the gate must not assume it
504	was. An *accepted* draft is the one that passed, which is not always the best.
505	
506	Two things that cost nothing and are worth doing. Tell the writer when it is on
507	its last allowed draft, because one that knows it spends its effort on the
508	findings rather than on flourishes. And after a redraft, check whether the
509	quoted passages are still present verbatim — if one survived, the repair did not
510	happen, and that is arithmetic rather than judgement.
511	
512	### Check the prose for what a script can see
513	
514	Before promoting a draft, run:
515	
516	```bash
517	python -m backend.chapters.check_prose output/<slug>/chapters/chNN.md
518	```
519	
520	It reports a sentence repeated word for word, a heading glued to the previous
521	line, and a paragraph echoing another's opening. **It does not gate.** There are
522	six characteristics, and this script is not a seventh. It never blocks a
523	chapter on its own — its count feeds `prose`, which does.
524	
525	What it finds, you fix the way you fix anything else: a literal substitution,
526	quoted, in the next sheet. A duplicated sentence is exactly the shape redraft
527	rule 2 wants — the quote is the identity, and removing it changes nothing the
528	findings did not name.
529	
530	What it **cannot** see is in its own output, under `not_checked`. A clean result
531	means three mechanical defects are absent, not that the prose is good. Nothing
532	here measures that.
533	
534	**Write its output to `critiques/chNN.prose.json`, clean or not.** A check whose
535	result exists only in this conversation cannot be read afterwards by anyone, and
536	"we ran it and it was fine" is not a record. A clean file is the evidence the
537	check ran at all — which is exactly why `length` and `chatter` get critique files
538	even though you computed them yourself.
539	
540	### Record it
541	
542	Write, for each chapter:
543	
544	- `chapters/ch0N.md` — the accepted draft
545	- `chapters/ch0N.summary.md` — a summary you write, under
546	  `context.max_summary_words`, which becomes part of the next chapter's rolling
547	  summary. This is the only channel between chapters, so it carries what a later
548	  chapter cannot be written without: what changed, who now knows what, and what
549	  is still open.
550	
551	  **Then run the chapter's checks, which include it:**
552	
553	```bash
554	  python -m backend.checks FLOW-4 output/<slug> <N>
555	```
556	
557	  The cap is the flat cost curve.
558	
559	  The Bible is fixed and the outline entry is one chapter's. **The summary is the
560	  only part of a chapter's packet that can grow with the book**, so
561	  `max_summary_words` is the whole of the claim that chapter thirty-four's prompt
562	  is the size of chapter one's.
563	
564	  It was being exceeded: on a real `small` run, five of six summaries were over
565	  the 200-word cap, the worst by 23%. A number nobody measures becomes a target
566	  rather than a limit.
567	
568	  **If it reports over, trim the NEXT one. Do not truncate a summary already
569	  written** — the cap protects a budget, and a dropped sentence loses the only
570	  channel between chapters, which costs more than the words saved.
571	- `critiques/ch0N.<critic>.json` — **one per characteristic, all five**,
572	  every iteration's score and findings, not just the last. `length` and
573	  `chatter` get files too even though you computed them yourself: recent runs
574	  folded those two into `chNN.gate.json` and wrote no file, and the measurement
575	  script then cannot see five scores and reports every chapter as never having
576	  passed. **The rejected draft's critique is the evidence that the gate did
577	  something**, and it is the first thing worth opening when someone asks whether
578	  this pipeline is real.
579	
580	  **The envelope is an object, not a bare array**, because the panel reads the
581	  fields around the iterations:
582	
583	  ```json
584	  {"critic": "continuity", "chapter": 2, "kind": "model",
585	   "agent": "continuity-critic", "drafts": 2,
586	   "iterations": [
587	     {"iteration": 1, "score": 4, "findings": [
588	       {"kind": "timeline-math", "severity": "high",
589	        "quote": "<copied from the draft>",
590	        "claim": "<what is wrong>",
591	        "fix": "<what would fix it>",
592	        "reference": "bible/timeline.md, Day 2"}]},
593	     {"iteration": 2, "score": 10, "findings": []}]}
594	  ```
595	
596	  A run wrote the array on its own, with `problem` where this says `claim`. Both
597	  are read now, but write this shape: the reader that had to be taught to accept
598	  the other one was taught after it had already put a blank page in front of
599	  someone.
600	
601	Append one row per subagent call to `logs/agents.jsonl`: timestamp, stage, agent,
602	chapter, iteration, verdict. Update `state.json` after each chapter so an
603	interrupted run can be resumed from the last accepted one rather than restarted.
604	
605	**Write the bookkeeping in the same reply that dispatches the next thing.** A
606	measured run spent twenty-five minutes of wall clock on twelve and a half
607	minutes of subagent work: half the run was the orchestrator between calls,
608	writing one file per reply. The critique files, the gate row, the log rows and
609	`state.json` for chapter *n* are all independent of each other and of chapter
610	*n*+1's draft, so issue them as parallel tool calls alongside the `Agent` call
611	that starts the next chapter. They then cost nothing at all, because the writer
612	is working while they are written.
613	
614	The one that cannot move is `chapters/ch0N.summary.md`. The next chapter's
615	prompt carries it, so it is written before that dispatch, not beside it.
616	
617	**And one `gate_decision` row per iteration, in the same log.** This is not
618	optional and it is not the same thing as the critique file. A run once wrote
619	complete, careful `chNN.gate.json` files and no gate rows, and the panel's whole
620	Quality screen was empty for a run whose gate had sent a chapter back and got a
621	better one — the work happened and the record of it was in a place nothing reads.
622	The shape:
623	
624	```json
625	{"ts":"...","event":"gate_decision","stage":"FLOW-4","chapter":2,"iteration":1,
626	 "scores":{"length":10,"chatter":10,"continuity":10,"science":6},
627	 "aggregate":6,"threshold":8,"verdict":"retry","note":"..."}
628	```
629	
630	`verdict` is `accept`, `retry`, `patched` or `halt` — these four words, not
631	`accepted`/`rejected`, and the `attempts` table's CHECK admits no others: write
632	anything else and the insert fails.
633	
634	**There is no verdict for "kept below the threshold".** That was
635	`accept_with_warnings`, which `patch_then_halt` replaced: a draft still under the
636	threshold after the patch does not get a row saying so and go into the book — it
637	gets `halt`, and the run stops. `patched` is the row for a draft the patch
638	brought up to the threshold: it passed, and it did not pass on its own, and a
639	reader is entitled to both facts.
640	
641	**Timestamp from a clock, not from an estimate.** The same run stamped its
642	twenty-four rows across twenty-four minutes and had actually taken seventy-two.
643	Nothing warned anybody, because a plausible number and a measured one look
644	identical once written down. Read the real time — `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`
645	— rather than working out what it probably is.
646	
647	**Record `tokens` and `model` on every agent row, for every stage.** The Agent
648	tool reports `subagent_tokens` in its result, and a task notification repeats it;
649	take the figure from there and write it down.
650	
651	`model` is the **full model id**, not the family word. The agent files say
652	`model: haiku` (SPEC-011) because Claude Code resolves that to whichever Haiku is
653	current; `config/pricing.json` is keyed by `claude-haiku-4-5` (and `claude-opus-5`,
654	`claude-sonnet-5` for the runs before it). Four
655	runs wrote `opus` and `sonnet`, no key matched, and every one of them showed no
656	cost at all — which reads as "this run was free" rather than "the name did not
657	match the price list". The panel now folds the family word in, but it can only do
658	that while there is exactly one Opus rate on file. Write the id.
659	
660	Three things about that figure, because getting them wrong makes the numbers
661	worse than absent:
662	
663	- **It is cumulative across a resume.** An agent sent back for a redraft reports
664	  the running total for the whole agent, not the cost of the second attempt. Log
665	  the *difference* from its previous total, so each row is one attempt.
666	- **It is a single total**, with no input/output split. Do not invent one.
667	- **A blocked or wasted call still costs.** Log it with its tokens and the reason
668	  it produced nothing. The first run of this pipeline spent 17,479 tokens on a
669	  rewrite the Write tool refused, and that is exactly the kind of number a
670	  dashboard exists to surface.
671	
672	Without these fields `tools/export_to_langfuse.py` ships the run with no usage
673	and no cost, and there is nothing to observe.
674	
675	## 5. FLOW-5 — style
676	
677	Dispatch `style-editor` for **every approved chapter in one message**. The
678	passes are independent — that is the whole premise of the stage, one voice
679	applied to chapters written in isolation — so there is no reason for chapter 3
680	to wait on chapter 1.
681	
682	Dispatch `publisher` in that same message. FLOW-6 is drawn after FLOW-5 in the
683	flow spec, but read what the synopsis is written from: the Bible, the outline and
684	the chapter summaries. None of those is touched by the style pass. Waiting for
685	the style passes to finish before starting it buys nothing and costs a round.
686	
687	**Check its work with arithmetic.** Count the words in what it returns and
688	compare with what you sent. If the counts differ, the pass rewrote something —
689	discard it and copy the unedited chapter to `ch0N.final.md` instead, and tell the
690	user which chapters that happened to. The published text must be the text the
691	gate approved.
692	
693	## 6. FLOW-6 — publish
694	
695	Dispatch `publisher` with the Bible, the outline and the chapter summaries — not
696	the chapters; a synopsis is written from canon. Give it
697	`outputs.synopsis.words.min/max` and `comparables`. Write the result to
698	`synopsis.md`. Dispatch it alongside the style passes, as FLOW-5 says: it reads
699	nothing they write.
700	
701	**Before assembling, run the book's checks:**
702	
703	```bash
704	python -m backend.checks FLOW-6 output/<slug>
705	```
706	
707	This is the last moment a promise landing in a chapter that was never written can
708	be found before a reader finds it.
709	
710	Then **assemble `dist/book.md` yourself**, in the shell, by concatenating the
711	`.final.md` files in order with the synopsis in front if
712	`outputs.markdown.include_synopsis` is true. Do not ask a subagent to do this.
713	Concatenation is a mechanical transformation, and a model asked to perform one
714	will paraphrase a sentence in the middle that the gate already approved.
715	
716	PDF export is not available in this architecture — it was a Python module, and
717	`outputs.formats` reads `["markdown"]` here. If a config asks for `pdf`, say so
718	plainly rather than producing something and calling it a PDF.
719	
720	## 7. Report
721	
722	Tell the user: the workspace path, **chapters that passed on their own versus
723	chapters that needed the patch**, total words, and the path of any chapter whose
724	style pass was discarded. Then name the file worth opening first — a
725	`critiques/*.json` from a chapter that was rejected once, because that is what
726	shows the gate working.
727	
728	That first figure used to read "approved versus accepted with warnings", which
729	was the old exit's vocabulary surviving in the report after it had been removed
730	from the gate. Under `patch_then_halt` nothing is accepted with warnings; either
731	a chapter reached the threshold or the run halted.
732	
733	---
734	
735	## Where the time goes
736	
737	Measured, on a three-chapter run that logged `duration_ms` on every call:
738	**nineteen subagent calls totalling twelve and a half minutes, inside
739	twenty-five minutes of wall clock.** Half the run was not the models at all. It
740	was the orchestrator between them — reading a file back, counting words, writing
741	a critique, appending a log row, one reply at a time.
742	
743	That changes where the work is. The subagent time is mostly irreducible without
744	giving something up; the other half is round trips, and round trips are free to
745	collapse.
746	
747	**What costs nothing.** Both critics in one reply. All style passes and the
748	publisher in one reply. The bookkeeping for chapter *n* in the same reply as the
749	dispatch for chapter *n*+1. Skipping the model critics on a draft that
750	failed `chatter`. None of these changes a word that reaches the reader, and
751	together they are worth more than any of the trades below.
752	
753	**What is not available.** The chapters cannot overlap. Chapter *n* is written
754	from the rolling summary of chapters 1..*n*-1, so starting two at once means
755	writing the second from a summary that does not exist yet. That is not a
756	scheduling detail — the summary chain is the only channel between chapters and
757	the reason the isolation is survivable at all. FLOW-1, 2 and 3 are sequential for
758	the same kind of reason: each is written from the one before.
759	
760	**What is worth knowing about the numbers.** The three Bible stages are the
761	slowest calls in the run — 101s, 135s and 77s — and they are also the three that
762	everything downstream is written from. They are the last place to economise.
763	Chapter drafts, by contrast, came back in about fifteen seconds each. A run is
764	not slow because the chapters are long.
765	
766	**What would be faster and would cost something.** Say which, plainly, rather
767	than doing any of it quietly:
768	
769	- a smaller model for the writer or the critics — fewer minutes, different prose,
770	  and a gate judged by a weaker judge
771	- fewer critics, or a lower threshold — fewer rounds only because fewer drafts
772	  get sent back
773	- one draft, no gate — roughly half the wall clock of a run that redrafts, and
774	  then the pipeline is a prompt with extra steps
775	
776	None of those is the orchestrator's decision to make.
777	
778	---
779	
780	## What this architecture does not give you
781	
782	State these when a reader asks what the pipeline guarantees. They are honest
783	limits, not caveats to bury.
784	
785	**The gate is not reproducible.** Two of the four critics are models. The same
786	draft can score 8 one run and 7 the next, so "it passed the gate" is a statement
787	about one run and not a property of the text. The `length` and `chatter` critics
788	*are* arithmetic and do reproduce.
789	
790	**There is no tamper-evident audit.** `logs/agents.jsonl` is a record you write,
791	not a hash chain, and anyone who can edit the file can edit it undetectably.
792	
793	**There is no enforced budget ceiling.** Nothing stops a run before it spends.
794	Read the call count out of the plan in step 0 and decide there.
795	
796	**It does not run unattended.** This is a procedure a person drives inside Claude
797	Code. It has no headless entry point and will not run in CI.
798	
799	The `main` branch of this repository holds the Python implementation, which has
800	all four of those and a byte-reproducible fixture. If what you need is an
801	auditable harness that runs on its own, that branch is the one — this one trades
802	those properties for subagents whose isolation is structural rather than
803	asserted.
804

file.content:
---
name: novaforge
description: Write a novel from a premise by orchestrating the ten NovaForge subagents through the six stages of specs/flow.yaml, with a per-chapter quality gate. Use when asked to draft, generate or continue a NovaForge novel, or when asked to run a stage of the pipeline.
---

# NovaForge — the orchestration procedure

You are the orchestrator. The ten agents in `.claude/agents/` are subagents
you dispatch with the Agent tool. This file is the procedure; `specs/flow.yaml`
is the contract it implements.

**The premise decides what kind of book this is.** Not this file, not the agent
files and not the config. All the agents used to open by declaring themselves
hard science fiction; none does now, and `novel.tone` is null until you set it.
Read the genre off the premise and carry it into every prompt.

**Read `specs/flow.yaml` and the config before you start.** They are not
decoration — the stage order, the gate thresholds and every number below come
from them, and they may have changed since this file was written. Where this
file and the spec disagree, the spec wins and you should say so.

## 0. Set up the run

Ask for, or take from the request:

- **the premise** — one or two sentences
- **the profile** — `tiny` (3 chapters), `small` (8), `medium` (18), `full` (34)

Then:

1. Read `config/novel.config.json`, then read `config/profiles/<profile>.json`
   and overlay it. A profile is partial: it states what it changes and nothing
   else, so overlay key by key rather than replacing whole sections. The profile
   overrides the whole `bible` block, and that matters: those counts are the
   size of the book's canon, and a three-chapter run handed a twelve-chapter
   Story Bible spends every chapter introducing things it has no room to use.

2. **Decide the genre and say so.** `novel.tone` is null unless somebody set it.
   Read it off the premise and write what you decided into the merged config
   before anything else runs.

   This is the single most consequential line in the run. It reaches every one
   of the agents, none of which has a genre of its own any more. It used
   to say `hard-scifi` permanently, and the results were exactly what you would
   expect: a cyberpunk premise came back as an engineering document with a
   bandwidth budget, and a premise about a pop star trying quesadillas came back
   unrecognisable. Name the genre the way a reader would — "cyberpunk noir,
   street level", "warm comic realism", "cosy mystery" — not the way a
   taxonomy would.

   Then, if the genre is not science fiction, **look at the critic list**.
   `quality_gate.critics` includes `science`, which is the world critic under a
   historical name: it audits the draft against the bullets under `## Rules` in
   `bible/world.md`, whatever kind of rules those are. That works for any genre
   as long as the rules are the story's own. What does not work is a world bible
   full of arithmetic in a story with no room for it — see FLOW-1.
3. Derive a slug from the premise — lowercase, hyphenated, at most 40
   characters — unless one was given.
4. Create the workspace: `output/<slug>/` with `bible/`, `chapters/`,
   `critiques/`, `dist/` and `logs/`.
5. Write the merged configuration to `output/<slug>/config.snapshot.json`. A run
   nobody can reconstruct the settings of is a run nobody can explain.
6. Write `output/<slug>/state.json` with the premise, the profile, the slug and
   an empty `chapters` list.

**Tell the user the plan before you spend anything**: the genre you read off the
premise, the profile, the chapter count, the target words per chapter and how
many subagent calls that implies. Put the genre first — it is the one they can
correct in a word, and the one that makes every other number worthless if it is
wrong.
A `full` run is thirty-four chapters through a gate — it is not a thing to start
by accident.

## 1. FLOW-1 — worldbuild

Dispatch `worldbuilder`. Its prompt must carry, because it has no Read tool:

- the premise, verbatim
- `novel.tone` — the genre you decided, in the words you decided it in
- `novel.chapters`
- the counts from `bible`: `factions`, `technology_entries`, `world_rules`,
  `world_min_words`, `world_max_words`
- the absolute path of the workspace, so it can write `bible/world.md`

When it returns, read `bible/world.md` yourself and check the `## Rules` heading
exists with at least `bible.world_rules.min` bullets under it. If it does not,
dispatch again with that as the correction. Nothing downstream can recover a
missing rules section: the science critic reads from under that heading and
nowhere else.

## 2. FLOW-2 — characters

Dispatch `character-architect`. Its prompt must carry the **full text of
`bible/world.md`** — it has no Read tool either — plus the premise, the tone,
and the counts for `characters`, `timeline_rows` and `mysteries`.

Carry `novel.names` too. It is passed to the agent verbatim and its default,
`familiar`, asks for names a reader can say out loud and tell apart. A run once
produced five four-syllable names inside fourteen hundred words, and a reader
who cannot keep the cast straight has already stopped reading.

It returns the canonical character names. **Keep that list.** Every later prompt
carries it, and it is what the continuity critic checks spelling against.

**Before leaving FLOW-2, run its checks:**

```bash
python -m backend.checks FLOW-2 output/<slug>
```

The Bible is now written and nothing has cited it yet. This is the cheapest
moment to find a rule with no number and a promise with no chapter, because every
later stage quotes both.

## 3. FLOW-3 — outline

Dispatch `plot-architect` with all four Bible files quoted in full, the chapter
count, the canonical names, and `novel.promises` and `novel.beats_per_chapter`.

It returns the outline as text. **You** write it to `output/<slug>/outline.md`.

**Run the stage's checks — one command, not a list you remember:**

```bash
python -m backend.checks FLOW-3 output/<slug>
```

It runs everything FLOW-3 owes and names whatever failed. Seven instruments now
stand between a run and a defect, and **remembering which at what moment is
exactly what has failed here**: a chapter promoted at 5, a summary cap exceeded
five times, a verdict written in a vocabulary the database rejects. None of those
was forgotten on purpose.

It reports; it does not gate. `decide` and `promote` are the only things that
refuse.

What it checks at this stage, and why each matters.

**`promises are reachable`.** `bible/mysteries.md` is the only part of the Bible
that commits to *when*: each
question names the chapter that plants it and the chapter that lands it. A
promise planted and never paid is the foreshadowing failure the ontology names,
and it is **the one literary defect a script can reach** — but only because the
Bible names chapters.

If it reports `unstated`, the promises exist and nothing can tell whether the
book keeps them; send `character-architect` back for the `Planted:` and `Lands:`
lines. If it reports a landing past the last chapter, the outline owes an answer
the book will not reach, and that is cheaper to fix now than at chapter eight.

**It reads the commitment, not the chapter.** A chapter that says nothing about
the mystery it was supposed to land passes this and fails a reader.

**`rules resolve`.** The critics and the audit refer to rules **by number** — *"R5 rewritten to name
the keeper as the writer"*. If `bible/world.md` writes them as unnumbered
bullets, those numbers are **the critic counting bullets and inventing an
identifier**, and two real runs produced 76 such references that resolved to
nothing. A positional reference points at a different rule the moment one is
inserted, and the arbitration record decays without anyone noticing.

If it reports `unnumbered`, send `worldbuilder` back to number them. Do not
renumber them yourself — the Bible has two authors and you are not one of them.

### Audit the commission before anyone writes it

Dispatch `science-critic` with the outline entries and `bible/world.md`, asking
it whether every beat can happen **without breaking a rule**. There is no draft;
it is judging the commission, not prose.

This is the cheapest check in the pipeline and it earns its place. Run against a
real outline it cost $0.07-$0.13 and found two defects the full five-critic gate
never caught across three attempts and a patch: a beat that had a field-team
member set a permanent RECOVERED line the rules reserve to the duty controller,
and a beat that fired an automatic callout at exactly twenty minutes when the
rule says more than twenty. Both were cheap to fix in the outline and expensive
to discover in a chapter.

Ask for a finding per violated clause, not per beat — a rule that says **who may
act, on what evidence, and within what window** is three clauses, and a beat can
satisfy the window while using evidence the rule never admitted.

**Also ask which rules are AMBIGUOUS, and treat that as a finding.** This is not
padding. A run deadlocked on a rule that read two ways: the science critic held
that a correction line needs its own two confirmations, three separate audits
held that it inherits the original line's, and both readings are defensible from
the same sentence. Two critics then pulled in opposite directions on the same
draft for three attempts and the chapter could not pass. An ambiguous rule does
not fail loudly; it fails as a disagreement nobody can arbitrate, and the place
to fix it is `bible/world.md`, before FLOW-4.

Where a beat is impossible or a rule reads two ways, dispatch `plot-architect`
again with that finding, or fix the rule, and do not start FLOW-4 on a commission
that contradicts canon. A chapter cannot be redrafted into obeying a rule its own
outline told it to break.

### Write the audit down in this exact shape

`output/<slug>/critiques/outline.audit.json`, and **these keys, spelled this
way**:

```json
{"stage": "FLOW-3", "agent": "science-critic", "ts": "<a real clock reading>",
 "verdict": "clean" | "defects",
 "violations":  [{"chapter": 3, "beat": 4, "rule": "R1", "clause": "...",
                  "severity": "high", "claim": "...", "fix": "...",
                  "arbitration": "UPHELD ... | OVERRULED ..."}],
 "ambiguities": [{"rule": "R5", "clause": "...", "reading_a": "...",
                  "reading_b": "...", "outline_assumes": "a" | "b" | "neither",
                  "arbitration": "...", "applied": "..."}]}
```

**Both arrays always, even when empty.** Two real runs wrote this file two
different ways — one used `ambiguities`, the other `ambiguous_rules` with a
`violations_note` beside an empty `violations` — and a reader that wants to ask
"how often does the audit find something" cannot, because the question has two
spellings. v1 wrote its critiques in three shapes for the same reason: nobody
said which. **A contract nobody stated cannot be enforced, and this is the
statement.**

Start every `arbitration` with `UPHELD` or `OVERRULED`. The word is read by a
script; the sentence after it is for a person.

Then split it on `### Chapter N — Title` and keep one entry per chapter. If the
split yields fewer entries than `novel.chapters`, the outline is malformed —
dispatch again rather than writing chapters from nothing. Anything other than
that exact heading shape, `**Chapter 1: Title**` most often, breaks the split.

## 4. FLOW-4 — chapters, with the gate

For each chapter `n` from 1 to `novel.chapters`:

### Assemble the writer's context — and nothing more

The prompt for `chapter-writer` contains exactly:

- the four Bible files, in full
- **this chapter's outline entry only**
- the rolling summary, capped at `context.max_summary_words` words
- the canonical character names
- the chapter number, its title, and `novel.words_per_chapter.target`

**It never contains a previous chapter's prose.** That is the architectural claim
of the project. Here it holds for two reasons that are worth keeping separate:
you do not put prose in the prompt, and the subagent has only `Glob`, which
returns paths and cannot return contents — so the guarantee does not rest solely
on your discipline. Do not add `Read` to that agent to make something easier.

### Run the gate

The critics are `quality_gate.critics` in the config. **Six now** — LOOP-003
added the fifth, SPEC-006 the sixth — and every one of them scores from the first
attempt:

| characteristic | who runs it | how |
|---|---|---|
| `continuity` | subagent | dispatch `continuity-critic` with the draft and the Bible |
| `science` | subagent | dispatch `science-critic` with the draft and `bible/world.md` |
| `outline` | subagent | dispatch `outline-critic` with the draft and **this chapter's outline entry, beats numbered** |
| `prose` | subagent | dispatch `prose-critic` with the draft, the genre and the tone |
| `length` | **you** | count words in the shell; score 10 inside the band, 0 outside |
| `chatter` | **you** | scan for preamble; score 0 if the draft does not begin with `# Chapter` |

`outline` exists because the others all ask whether the draft is *correct* and
none asks whether it is *the chapter the outline commissioned*. A draft that is
consistent with the Bible, obeys the world, sits in the word band and is about
something else entirely used to pass this gate cleanly.

**`prose` asks the question none of the other five ask: is it well written?** It
returns quoted `major` and `minor` findings and **no score**. You do not compute
one either — you ask:

```bash
echo '{"major": <n>, "minor": <n>}'   | python -m backend.chapters.score_prose       output/<slug>/chapters/chNN.attemptK.md output/<slug>/bible/characters.md
```

It runs the mechanical check itself and applies

```
prose = 10 − 3·mechanical − 2·major − 1·minor,   floored at 0
```

returning the score, its arithmetic in `why`, and the mechanical defects quoted
so you can put them in the sheet.

**You supply only the two counts, because they are the only part you know.** The
mechanical term is not an input: a critic asked to count what a script already
counted will disagree with it, and then the score depends on which of the two you
asked. If the critic reports a mechanical defect anyway, drop it — it is already
charged, and one fault charged twice costs the chapter six points instead of
three.

**Count only findings the critic actually quoted.** A finding without a quote
cannot be sent to the writer and cannot be verified afterwards, so it is not a
finding; say so in the gate row rather than letting it lower a score in silence.

**Check the critic's own arithmetic against what it quoted**, as you do for
`outline`. Its `notes` state its counts; the findings are what it can defend.

Dispatch the four critic subagents **in the same message**, as four tool calls in
one reply. Not "one after the other quickly" — in the same reply. They are
independent, they judge a text that is already fixed, and nothing either returns
changes what the other is asked.

This is the easiest minute in the run to lose, and it keeps being lost. Two runs
have now been measured: the first ran them in series in two chapters out of
four, the second in three out of four. In the second run continuity and science
started fifty seconds apart on chapter 2 and thirty seconds apart on chapter 3,
and each of those gaps is one critic finishing before the other was asked.

Check yourself afterwards: subtract the two `ts` values you logged for a
chapter's critics. If they are more than a few seconds apart they ran in series,
and that is a fact worth writing in the row's `note` rather than one to leave
for whoever reads the log later.

Run `length` and `chatter` **first**, before dispatching anything, because they
are arithmetic and cost nothing. If `chatter` scores 0 — the draft does not begin
with `# Chapter`, so it is not a chapter yet — redraft on that alone and do not
spend two model calls judging the prose of something that has to be rebuilt
anyway. Do *not* take the same shortcut when only `length` fails: an off-band
draft is still a chapter, and the continuity and science findings are what the
redraft is steered by. Skipping them there buys a minute and spends it on a
worse second draft.

Count words with a command, never by eye:

```bash
wc -w < output/<slug>/chapters/ch0N.md
```

The band is `words_per_chapter.min` to `.max`, widened by `tolerance_pct`.

Aggregate with `quality_gate.aggregate` — `min`, so **a chapter is only as good
as its worst characteristic**. A chapter passes when **all five are at 8 or
above**, not when the average is.

**Write every attempt's draft to `chapters/ch0N.attemptK.md` before you score
it.** This is not bookkeeping. The rejected drafts are the only thing "the
writer changed only what was cited" can be measured from, and a run that
overwrites them has destroyed the evidence rather than saved a file. The
measurement script reports that as *not measurable*, which is the honest answer
and a useless one.

### The three attempts, and why the third is different

`quality_gate.max_revisions` is 2, so there are three attempts. The principle
LOOP-003 runs on is that **each failed attempt must make the next one easier,
not merely better informed.** So the feedback escalates in concreteness until
there is nothing left to interpret:

| attempt | what the writer gets | what it is asked to do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the Bible, its outline entry, the rolling summary | write the chapter |
| 2 | the above, plus a **level-1 sheet**: per finding, the exact quote, what is wrong, against what, and *how it should read* — described, not written | correct only what is marked, touching as few lines as possible |
| 3 | the above, plus a **level-2 sheet**: per open finding, **the literal replacement sentence, written by the critic** | integrate those sentences; do not rewrite |

On the second attempt the writer interprets a description. On the third it does
not interpret at all — it integrates a given text. And if even that fails:

**You do not work out what happens next. You ask, and you obey.** After every
scored attempt, run:

```bash
echo '{"aggregate": <min>, "attempt": <n>, "patched": <true|false>}' \
  | python -m backend.chapters.decide
```

It answers `accept`, `retry`, `patch` or `halt`, with its reason. **Do what it
says, including when you disagree with it.** If you think it is wrong, say so to
the user in the report — do not act on the disagreement.

This used to be a paragraph you read and applied yourself, and it was moved into
code deliberately (SPEC-004). You read it at the worst possible moment: a run has
been going for an hour and is about to be thrown away. That is exactly when "it
is only just below" gets rationalised, and `accept_with_warnings` — the exit this
replaced, which put a chapter that had failed three times into the book with a
note in the margin — is what rationalising looks like when it wins.

What each answer asks of you:

- **`accept`** — promote it, and **do not write `chapters/chNN.md` yourself**:

  ```bash
  python -m backend.chapters.promote output/<slug> <N>
  ```

  It re-reads the chapter's critiques, recomputes the aggregate, asks `decide`
  again and copies the draft **only on `accept`**. On anything else it refuses,
  exits non-zero and leaves the file untouched.

  That is deliberate belt and braces. On a real run a chapter scored 5 and was
  copied into the book anyway — no third attempt, no patch, no halt — because
  writing that file was a one-line copy and nothing stood between the copy and
  the book. You still hold `Write` and can always do it by hand; the point is
  that the correct path is now the shorter one, and the incorrect one requires
  choosing it.

  If the answer's `verdict` is `patched`, record `patched`, not `accept`: it
  passed, and it did not pass on its own.
- **`retry`** — redraft against the sheet at the level the reason names.
- **`patch`** — apply the critics' own replacement sentences by literal
  substitution, then rescore. For `length` and `chatter` this is trivial — trim
  words, fix the first line. For the three model characteristics it is the
  sentence the critic proposed, which you **arbitrate before applying**: you have
  overruled a false finding before, and a replacement built on one would write
  the error into the book by hand. Then ask again with `"patched": true`.
- **`halt`** — **stop the run.** Do not promote the chapter, do not run FLOW-5 or
  FLOW-6. By construction the only way to arrive here is a critic's replacement
  that was itself wrong and that arbitration did not catch, and that is worth a
  person looking at before another chapter is written.

**Where this guarantee is weakest, said plainly:** `outline` is the hardest to
patch, because a missing beat is not a sentence but a paragraph. Its level-2
replacement is that paragraph, written by the critic in the book's voice. That
is a larger thing to insert blind than a corrected clause, and it is the part of
"it will pass by the third" that rests on the most.

### The sheet

`specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheet_template/v01.md` is the format and it does not vary.
Fill it, then **run `node specs/loops/LOOP-003/validate-sheet.mjs <file>` and do
not send a sheet that fails.** An unsent sheet is a bug caught; a half-filled one
is an attempt wasted, because a writer without the quote is back to guessing,
which is the state attempt 1 was already in.

Five rules the sheet obeys, each of which is in the validator:

1. **All six scores, including the passing ones.** The writer has to know what
   is already right in order to leave it alone.
2. **An explicit DO NOT TOUCH list.** In the saved run the writer changed two
   lines and then one. That restraint is the thing to protect: a writer that
   takes the opportunity to improve an approved paragraph is the commonest way
   a score that was passing stops passing.
3. **Four fields per finding** — quote, what is wrong, against what, how it
   should read — or it does not go. The quote is literal. "Against what" points
   at the Bible or the outline, **never at a previous chapter**: the writer has
   never seen one, and this sheet is not the hole through which it finally does.
4. **A RESOLVED list.** The writer learns what worked, and so does the loop —
   which phrasing of "how it should read" produced a correction first time is
   the only thing this loop actually learns.
5. **Every finding, worst first, none trimmed.** A finding held back to keep the
   sheet short is a finding that fails again next attempt.

Write each sheet to **`specs/loops/LOOP-003/sheets/<slug>/chNN.attemptK.md`** as
you send it. The slug is not decoration: the flat path has no run dimension, and
the second run to use this loop silently overwrote the first's chapter 1 and
chapter 3 sheets. They were recoverable from git and were restored byte-exact,
which is luck. The sheets are the only record of what the writer was actually
told, and §8.1 of LOOP-003 says the one thing this loop learns is read out of
them.

### The late finding

A critic that raises something on the third attempt which was equally present in
the first draft, and said nothing then, has moved the goalposts. Mark that
finding **late**: record it in `specs/loops/LOOP-003/late_findings.jsonl`, patch
it if you can, and **do not let it block the chapter**.

Without this rule the third-attempt guarantee does not exist, because something
new can always appear. A critic that accumulates late findings is a critic that
does not read the same way twice, and that is a problem to fix in the critic
rather than in the chapter.

### Four rules for the redraft, each of which was once got wrong

These were found by running the pipeline, not by reading it. Every one of them
made the gate weaker in a way that looked like it was working.

**1. Hand back the draft, not only the findings.** A redraft prompt that carries
the findings without the text they quote is asking for "repair these and change
nothing else" when there is nothing to change — so the writer starts a fresh
chapter each round, against findings quoting text that is no longer in it, and a
rewrite can come back worse than what it replaced.

This is not a hole in the context policy, and the distinction is the whole
point: the policy forbids a **previous chapter's** prose. This is the writer's
own rejected draft of the chapter it is writing now.

**2. Ask for substitutions, not for a chapter.** Rather than the whole chapter
back, ask for the exact sentences to replace:

```json
{"patches": [{"find": "<text copied EXACTLY from the draft>",
              "replace": "<the corrected text>",
              "why": "<which finding this addresses>"}]}
```

Apply them yourself, matching `find` literally. Two things follow: anything the
findings do not name **cannot** change, because you do not touch it; and "was
this finding addressed" stops being a judgement — either the quoted text is
still there or it is not. A `find` that does not match is skipped and counted,
never applied approximately. If no patch applies at all, fall back to a full
rewrite rather than burning the attempt on nothing, and record which happened.

**3. A critic that returns no usable verdict is excluded, never counted as a
pass.** If `continuity-critic` or `science-critic` comes back with something you
cannot parse as a score, do not substitute one: 10 invents an approval and 0
invents a rejection. Leave it out of the `min`, record it as unscored, and say
so in the gate row's `note`. A gate running on three critics is weaker than one
running on four, and that is the truth of what happened.

**4. Keep the best draft, not the last.** Track the highest aggregate as you go.
A chapter whose first draft scored 7 and whose third scored 4 must ship the 7 —
a rewrite is not guaranteed to be an improvement and the gate must not assume it
was. An *accepted* draft is the one that passed, which is not always the best.

Two things that cost nothing and are worth doing. Tell the writer when it is on
its last allowed draft, because one that knows it spends its effort on the
findings rather than on flourishes. And after a redraft, check whether the
quoted passages are still present verbatim — if one survived, the repair did not
happen, and that is arithmetic rather than judgement.

### Check the prose for what a script can see

Before promoting a draft, run:

```bash
python -m backend.chapters.check_prose output/<slug>/chapters/chNN.md
```

It reports a sentence repeated word for word, a heading glued to the previous
line, and a paragraph echoing another's opening. **It does not gate.** There are
six characteristics, and this script is not a seventh. It never blocks a
chapter on its own — its count feeds `prose`, which does.

What it finds, you fix the way you fix anything else: a literal substitution,
quoted, in the next sheet. A duplicated sentence is exactly the shape redraft
rule 2 wants — the quote is the identity, and removing it changes nothing the
findings did not name.

What it **cannot** see is in its own output, under `not_checked`. A clean result
means three mechanical defects are absent, not that the prose is good. Nothing
here measures that.

**Write its output to `critiques/chNN.prose.json`, clean or not.** A check whose
result exists only in this conversation cannot be read afterwards by anyone, and
"we ran it and it was fine" is not a record. A clean file is the evidence the
check ran at all — which is exactly why `length` and `chatter` get critique files
even though you computed them yourself.

### Record it

Write, for each chapter:

- `chapters/ch0N.md` — the accepted draft
- `chapters/ch0N.summary.md` — a summary you write, under
  `context.max_summary_words`, which becomes part of the next chapter's rolling
  summary. This is the only channel between chapters, so it carries what a later
  chapter cannot be written without: what changed, who now knows what, and what
  is still open.

  **Then run the chapter's checks, which include it:**

```bash
  python -m backend.checks FLOW-4 output/<slug> <N>
```

  The cap is the flat cost curve.

  The Bible is fixed and the outline entry is one chapter's. **The summary is the
  only part of a chapter's packet that can grow with the book**, so
  `max_summary_words` is the whole of the claim that chapter thirty-four's prompt
  is the size of chapter one's.

  It was being exceeded: on a real `small` run, five of six summaries were over
  the 200-word cap, the worst by 23%. A number nobody measures becomes a target
  rather than a limit.

  **If it reports over, trim the NEXT one. Do not truncate a summary already
  written** — the cap protects a budget, and a dropped sentence loses the only
  channel between chapters, which costs more than the words saved.
- `critiques/ch0N.<critic>.json` — **one per characteristic, all five**,
  every iteration's score and findings, not just the last. `length` and
  `chatter` get files too even though you computed them yourself: recent runs
  folded those two into `chNN.gate.json` and wrote no file, and the measurement
  script then cannot see five scores and reports every chapter as never having
  passed. **The rejected draft's critique is the evidence that the gate did
  something**, and it is the first thing worth opening when someone asks whether
  this pipeline is real.

  **The envelope is an object, not a bare array**, because the panel reads the
  fields around the iterations:

  ```json
  {"critic": "continuity", "chapter": 2, "kind": "model",
   "agent": "continuity-critic", "drafts": 2,
   "iterations": [
     {"iteration": 1, "score": 4, "findings": [
       {"kind": "timeline-math", "severity": "high",
        "quote": "<copied from the draft>",
        "claim": "<what is wrong>",
        "fix": "<what would fix it>",
        "reference": "bible/timeline.md, Day 2"}]},
     {"iteration": 2, "score": 10, "findings": []}]}
  ```

  A run wrote the array on its own, with `problem` where this says `claim`. Both
  are read now, but write this shape: the reader that had to be taught to accept
  the other one was taught after it had already put a blank page in front of
  someone.

Append one row per subagent call to `logs/agents.jsonl`: timestamp, stage, agent,
chapter, iteration, verdict. Update `state.json` after each chapter so an
interrupted run can be resumed from the last accepted one rather than restarted.

**Write the bookkeeping in the same reply that dispatches the next thing.** A
measured run spent twenty-five minutes of wall clock on twelve and a half
minutes of subagent work: half the run was the orchestrator between calls,
writing one file per reply. The critique files, the gate row, the log rows and
`state.json` for chapter *n* are all independent of each other and of chapter
*n*+1's draft, so issue them as parallel tool calls alongside the `Agent` call
that starts the next chapter. They then cost nothing at all, because the writer
is working while they are written.

The one that cannot move is `chapters/ch0N.summary.md`. The next chapter's
prompt carries it, so it is written before that dispatch, not beside it.

**And one `gate_decision` row per iteration, in the same log.** This is not
optional and it is not the same thing as the critique file. A run once wrote
complete, careful `chNN.gate.json` files and no gate rows, and the panel's whole
Quality screen was empty for a run whose gate had sent a chapter back and got a
better one — the work happened and the record of it was in a place nothing reads.
The shape:

```json
{"ts":"...","event":"gate_decision","stage":"FLOW-4","chapter":2,"iteration":1,
 "scores":{"length":10,"chatter":10,"continuity":10,"science":6},
 "aggregate":6,"threshold":8,"verdict":"retry","note":"..."}
```

`verdict` is `accept`, `retry`, `patched` or `halt` — these four words, not
`accepted`/`rejected`, and the `attempts` table's CHECK admits no others: write
anything else and the insert fails.

**There is no verdict for "kept below the threshold".** That was
`accept_with_warnings`, which `patch_then_halt` replaced: a draft still under the
threshold after the patch does not get a row saying so and go into the book — it
gets `halt`, and the run stops. `patched` is the row for a draft the patch
brought up to the threshold: it passed, and it did not pass on its own, and a
reader is entitled to both facts.

**Timestamp from a clock, not from an estimate.** The same run stamped its
twenty-four rows across twenty-four minutes and had actually taken seventy-two.
Nothing warned anybody, because a plausible number and a measured one look
identical once written down. Read the real time — `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`
— rather than working out what it probably is.

**Record `tokens` and `model` on every agent row, for every stage.** The Agent
tool reports `subagent_tokens` in its result, and a task notification repeats it;
take the figure from there and write it down.

`model` is the **full model id**, not the family word. The agent files say
`model: haiku` (SPEC-011) because Claude Code resolves that to whichever Haiku is
current; `config/pricing.json` is keyed by `claude-haiku-4-5` (and `claude-opus-5`,
`claude-sonnet-5` for the runs before it). Four
runs wrote `opus` and `sonnet`, no key matched, and every one of them showed no
cost at all — which reads as "this run was free" rather than "the name did not
match the price list". The panel now folds the family word in, but it can only do
that while there is exactly one Opus rate on file. Write the id.

Three things about that figure, because getting them wrong makes the numbers
worse than absent:

- **It is cumulative across a resume.** An agent sent back for a redraft reports
  the running total for the whole agent, not the cost of the second attempt. Log
  the *difference* from its previous total, so each row is one attempt.
- **It is a single total**, with no input/output split. Do not invent one.
- **A blocked or wasted call still costs.** Log it with its tokens and the reason
  it produced nothing. The first run of this pipeline spent 17,479 tokens on a
  rewrite the Write tool refused, and that is exactly the kind of number a
  dashboard exists to surface.

Without these fields `tools/export_to_langfuse.py` ships the run with no usage
and no cost, and there is nothing to observe.

## 5. FLOW-5 — style

Dispatch `style-editor` for **every approved chapter in one message**. The
passes are independent — that is the whole premise of the stage, one voice
applied to chapters written in isolation — so there is no reason for chapter 3
to wait on chapter 1.

Dispatch `publisher` in that same message. FLOW-6 is drawn after FLOW-5 in the
flow spec, but read what the synopsis is written from: the Bible, the outline and
the chapter summaries. None of those is touched by the style pass. Waiting for
the style passes to finish before starting it buys nothing and costs a round.

**Check its work with arithmetic.** Count the words in what it returns and
compare with what you sent. If the counts differ, the pass rewrote something —
discard it and copy the unedited chapter to `ch0N.final.md` instead, and tell the
user which chapters that happened to. The published text must be the text the
gate approved.

## 6. FLOW-6 — publish

Dispatch `publisher` with the Bible, the outline and the chapter summaries — not
the chapters; a synopsis is written from canon. Give it
`outputs.synopsis.words.min/max` and `comparables`. Write the result to
`synopsis.md`. Dispatch it alongside the style passes, as FLOW-5 says: it reads
nothing they write.

**Before assembling, run the book's checks:**

```bash
python -m backend.checks FLOW-6 output/<slug>
```

This is the last moment a promise landing in a chapter that was never written can
be found before a reader finds it.

Then **assemble `dist/book.md` yourself**, in the shell, by concatenating the
`.final.md` files in order with the synopsis in front if
`outputs.markdown.include_synopsis` is true. Do not ask a subagent to do this.
Concatenation is a mechanical transformation, and a model asked to perform one
will paraphrase a sentence in the middle that the gate already approved.
