# Chapter 9 — The Question Answered

The kitchen was the same as always—the long table, the light through the western window turning everything honey-colored, the smell of his mother's bread and olive oil. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] sat in his regular place, still dusty from the hill, and nobody said anything about the dirt on the chair. His mother had filled his plate without asking what he wanted. His father sat across from him the way he always did. Marcos was in the corner chair, the one that faced both the table and the door, watching the evening come in.

They ate without much talking at first—just the sound of forks, the clink of water glasses, his mother asking his father something about the shutters that needed fixing. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was hungrier than he had ever been. Everything tasted like itself: the bread was bread, salt was salt, the cheese was exactly what cheese was supposed to be. He thought about Clara's kitchen, about the meal there that morning—Elena handing him a thick cup of milk, Clara setting down a plate without fuss—and then he thought about sitting in this kitchen instead, and how it was the same shape of kindness but different in its details, in the way his mother folded her napkin and the particular creak of this chair under his weight.

"You'll want to tell Rosa everything," his mother said. Not a question.

"She won't forgive me if I don't," he said.

His father laughed—a real laugh, not a polite one. "She had a point about the feast ovens keeping her here."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nodded and kept eating. The sun was lower now, the light different. He thought about yesterday, about the moment the sun had touched the horizon and he had understood, really understood, that he could not go further down the hill into the dark. It had been frightening—that moment when the rules and the fear had suddenly meant the same thing. But then Clara had opened the door, and Elena had been there, and fear had become something else. A thing that happened and then was over. The dark had come all around him in that house, in that bed that wasn't his bed, and it had not swallowed him. Bruno had slept at the foot of it, breathing steady. And when the light came back, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was still himself, unchanged in any way that mattered.

He lifted his glass and drank. The water was cold. His father was talking about the weather, about whether the heat would break before September. His mother was not really listening; she was watching [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] in that way she had that made him feel known. Marcos was silent, tapping his stick twice against the leg of his chair—not tapping it to say something, just tapping it the way he did when he was thinking. The rhythm of supper. The rhythm that had held his place all night while he was gone.

After they had eaten, after his mother had cleared the plates and brought out the figs they always had at this hour, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] excused himself. His mother nodded. Nobody asked where he was going. He climbed the stairs to his room in the half-dark—twilight now, the last real light draining out of the day—and closed the door quietly.

Bruno was already on the bed, waiting. The dog lifted his head when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] came in, and when the boy lay down and turned toward the wall, Bruno jumped down and circled. Once, twice, three times—that was his way, the habit of settling that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had never thought much about until now. But this time, when Bruno circled, there was no tension in it. No unease held in his body. He was circling because that was what Bruno did, the same way a person might take a particular path to a familiar place. His tail was not tucked; his ears were not pinned back. When he lay down at the foot of the bed, he sighed—a small dog sigh, almost content—and rested his chin on his paws.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could feel the difference. Bruno knew something that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s own body was only just learning: that the danger was over. That the dark had been survived. That the world was still the same shape it had always been.

The light went on fading. His room became shades of grey and then something softer than that, something between blue and nothing. On the shelf, Captain Crunch caught what little light was left and seemed to glow—though it was only the pale limestone picking up the last glow from the western sky. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] thought about Elena's fossil on Clara's shelf, the spiral pale as bone, the way they had stood together looking at both of them, at the two things pulled from the earth that neither of them had made and both of them had kept.

He reached for his notebook. The leather one Marcos had given him, that first morning when he turned ten. He had asked a question on the first page and never gone back to it. Now he opened to a fresh page and found the pencil in the spine where he always kept it. The light was almost gone but there was enough, there was enough for this. He pressed the pencil to paper and began to write, the letters small and careful:

*Elena has a fossil too. We are the same kind of person.*

The pencil moved across the page and the words took their place, one after the other, true and solid on the paper, exactly as he had meant them to be.

The kitchen was the same as always—the long table, the light through the western window turning everything honey-colored, the smell of his mother's bread and olive oil. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] sat in his regular place, still dusty from the hill, and nobody said anything about the dirt on the chair. His mother had filled his plate without asking what he wanted. His father sat across from him the way he always did. Marcos was in the corner chair, the one that faced both the table and the door, watching the evening come in.

They ate without much talking at first—just the sound of forks, the clink of water glasses, his mother asking his father something about the shutters that needed fixing. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was hungrier than he had ever been. Everything tasted like itself: the bread was bread, salt was salt, the cheese was exactly what cheese was supposed to be. He thought about Clara's kitchen, about the meal there that morning—Elena handing him a thick cup of milk, Clara setting down a plate without fuss—and then he thought about sitting in this kitchen instead, and how it was the same shape of kindness but different in its details, in the way his mother folded her napkin and the particular creak of this chair under his weight.

"You'll want to tell Rosa everything," his mother said. Not a question.

"She won't forgive me if I don't," he said.

His father laughed—a real laugh, not a polite one. "She had a point about the feast ovens keeping her here."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nodded and kept eating. The sun was lower now, the light different. He thought about yesterday, about the moment the sun had touched the horizon and he had understood, really understood, that he could not go further down the hill into the dark. It had been frightening—that moment when the rules and the fear had suddenly meant the same thing. But then Clara had opened the door, and Elena had been there, and fear had become something else. A thing that happened and then was over. The dark had come all around him in that house, in that bed that wasn't his bed, and it had not swallowed him. Bruno had slept at the foot of it, breathing steady. And when the light came back, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was still himself, unchanged in any way that mattered.

He lifted his glass and drank. The water was cold. His father was talking about the weather, about whether the heat would break before September. His mother was not really listening; she was watching [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] in that way she had that made him feel known. Marcos was silent, tapping his stick twice against the leg of his chair—not tapping it to say something, just tapping it the way he did when he was thinking. The rhythm of supper. The rhythm that had held his place all night while he was gone.

After they had eaten, after his mother had cleared the plates and brought out the figs they always had at this hour, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] excused himself. His mother nodded. Nobody asked where he was going. He climbed the stairs to his room in the half-dark—twilight now, the last real light draining out of the day—and closed the door quietly.

Bruno was already on the bed, waiting. The dog lifted his head when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] came in, and when the boy lay down and turned toward the wall, Bruno jumped down and circled. Once, twice, three times—that was his way, the habit of settling that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had never thought much about until now. But this time, when Bruno circled, there was no tension in it. No unease held in his body. He was circling because that was what Bruno did, the same way a person might take a particular path to a familiar place. His tail was not tucked; his ears were not pinned back. When he lay down at the foot of the bed, he sighed—a small dog sigh, almost content—and rested his chin on his paws.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could feel the difference. Bruno knew something that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s own body was only just learning: that the danger was over. That the dark had been survived. That the world was still the same shape it had always been.

The light went on fading. His room became shades of grey and then something softer than that, something between blue and nothing. On the shelf, Captain Crunch caught what little light was left and seemed to glow—though it was only the pale limestone picking up the last glow from the western sky. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] thought about Elena's fossil on Clara's shelf, the spiral pale as bone, the way they had stood together looking at both of them, at the two things pulled from the earth that neither of them had made and both of them had kept.

Now he opened to a fresh page and found the pencil in the spine where he always kept it. The light was almost gone but there was enough, there was enough for this. He pressed the pencil to paper and began to write, the letters small and careful:

*Elena has a fossil too. We are the same kind of person.*

# Chapter 9 — The Question Answered

The kitchen was the same as always—the long table, the light through the western window turning everything honey-colored, the smell of his mother's bread and olive oil. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] sat in his regular place, still dusty from the hill, and nobody said anything about the dirt on the chair. His mother had filled his plate without asking what he wanted. His father sat across from him the way he always did. Marcos was in the corner chair, the one that faced both the table and the door, watching the evening come in.

They ate without much talking at first—just the sound of forks, the clink of water glasses, his mother asking his father something about the shutters that needed fixing. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was hungrier than he had ever been. Everything tasted like itself: the bread was bread, salt was salt, the cheese was exactly what cheese was supposed to be. He thought about Clara's kitchen, about the meal there that morning—Elena handing him a thick cup of milk, Clara setting down a plate without fuss—and then he thought about sitting in this kitchen instead, and how it was the same shape of kindness but different in its details, in the way his mother folded her napkin and the particular creak of this chair under his weight.

"You'll want to tell Rosa everything," his mother said. Not a question.

"She won't forgive me if I don't," he said.

His father laughed—a real laugh, not a polite one. "She had a point about the feast ovens keeping her here."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] nodded and kept eating. The sun was lower now, the light different. He thought about yesterday, about the moment the sun had touched the horizon and he had understood, really understood, that he could not go further down the hill into the dark. It had been frightening—that moment when the rules and the fear had suddenly meant the same thing. But then Clara had opened the door, and Elena had been there, and fear had become something else. A thing that happened and then was over. The dark had come all around him in that house, in that bed that wasn't his bed, and it had not swallowed him. Bruno had slept at the foot of it, breathing steady. And when the light came back, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was still himself, unchanged in any way that mattered.

He lifted his glass and drank. The water was cold. His father was talking about the weather, about whether the heat would break before September. His mother was not really listening; she was watching [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] in that way she had that made him feel known. Marcos was silent in his corner, one hand resting on his walking stick, his eyes on [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]. The rhythm of supper. The rhythm that had held his place all night while he was gone.

After they had eaten, after his mother had cleared the plates and brought out the figs they always had at this hour, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] excused himself. His mother nodded. Nobody asked where he was going. He climbed the stairs to his room in the half-dark—twilight now, the last real light draining out of the day—and closed the door quietly.

Bruno was already on the bed, waiting. The dog lifted his head when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] came in, and when the boy lay down and turned toward the wall, Bruno jumped down and circled. Once, twice, three times—that was his way, the habit of settling that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had never thought much about until now. But this time, when Bruno circled, there was no tension in it. He was circling because that was what Bruno did, his body loose and easy, the way he always settled in to sleep. When he lay down at the foot of the bed, he sighed—a small dog sigh, almost content—and rested his chin on his paws.

When Bruno lay down at the foot of the bed, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could feel the difference right away. His tail was straight, his ears forward, not pinned back. And his whole body—it wasn't coiled and ready anymore, waiting for something to happen. He was just Bruno, settling in to sleep the way he always did when nothing was wrong. The night was the same as any other night for him. So it was the same for [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] too.

The light went on fading. His room became shades of grey and then something softer than that, something between blue and nothing. On the shelf, Captain Crunch caught what little light was left and seemed to glow—though it was only the pale limestone picking up the last glow from the western sky. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] thought about Elena's fossil on Clara's shelf, the spiral pale as bone, the way they had stood together looking at both of them, at the two things pulled from the earth that neither of them had made and both of them had kept.

He reached for his notebook. The leather one Marcos had given him, that first morning when he turned ten. He had asked a question on the first page and never gone back to it. Now he opened to a fresh page and found the pencil in the spine where he always kept it. The light was almost gone but there was enough, there was enough for this. He pressed the pencil to paper and began to write, the letters small and careful:

*Elena has a fossil too. We are the same kind of person.*

The pencil moved across the page and the words took their place, one after the other, true and solid on the paper, exactly as he had meant them to be.

Days 1-5. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turned ten. Marcos, his grandfather, gave him a leather notebook for questions; two summers ago the two of them built the cardboard observatory that still stands in the garden. His father gave permission for the hill on one rule: home before the sun touches the horizon. He said he was afraid of nothing; nobody believed him. Rosa could not come — the feast ovens — and made him promise to tell her everything. Asked what lay beyond the hill, Marcos told a story instead of a fact, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said it wasn't fair.

Day 4 he climbed with Bruno. In deep shade Bruno whined against his leg; he said aloud that what frightened him was being lost and not getting Bruno home — not the dark — and went on anyway. Over the crest: a valley nobody mentions, a stone house, and Elena, twelve, who lives there with her grandmother Clara. The sun touched the horizon, so he stopped, as the rule says, and slept there. Elena has a fossil too, a pale spiral from the riverbed; he set Captain Crunch beside it and left her his striped grey stone.

Day 5 they walked down at dawn. He came home to both parents and a plate kept warm all night. Asked directly, Marcos said he had always known Elena's house was there and wanted him to find it himself. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was angry, and then neither of them looked away.

At supper that evening, all of them together, the dark turned out not to be the thing he feared. Bruno settled without tension. He wrote in his notebook: "Elena has a fossil too."

Nothing is open.

Elena has a fossil too, a pale spiral from the riverbed; he set Captain Crunch beside it and left her his striped grey stone.

Write Chapter 10 — the last chapter — of a ten-chapter novel. Return ONLY the chapter text, beginning with the line `# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now`. No preamble, no commentary, no notes afterwards.

GENRE AND TONE:
a warm, funny children's adventure — a read-aloud summer quest told close to the ground, brave and kind; small real wonders rather than magic, a dog who is a character, and a fear of the dark taken seriously and gently.

TARGET LENGTH: 1250 words. The accepted band is 1000–1500 words (hard limits after tolerance: 900–1650). Aim at 1250 and do not come in under 1100 — the previous chapter ran short and this one is the last, so it must not feel thin.

CANONICAL NAMES — spell them exactly, and use no others for these people:
[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] (the boy, ten years old — this literal bracketed token IS his name in this manuscript; write it exactly as `[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]`, every time, never substitute a real name)
Bruno (the terrier) · Marcos (the grandfather) · Rosa (the baker's daughter) · Elena (the girl on the other side, twelve) · Clara (Elena's grandmother) · Captain Crunch (the fossil)

# The World of The Other Side of the Hill

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] lives in a house at the edge of a small village in a landscape of stone and scrub, where the Mediterranean heat eases in the evening and the cicadas know when to start their song. The house is old enough to have stories but young enough to still live in them. Behind it rises a hill that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has never crossed, though he has stood at its foot a hundred times and wondered what a person might find there. This summer, the summer he turns ten, he is old enough—or brave enough, or curious enough—to go and see. His scruffy terrier Bruno will come with him. His fossil, his stones, his grandfather's cardboard observatory, and the dark that waits when the sun goes down: all of these are part of the story of that crossing.

## Places

- **The House and Garden** — A stone house with a wide kitchen where the family gathers. The garden is dry and full of olive trees, wild rosemary, and the long shadow the house casts on summer afternoons. The cardboard observatory stands near the back wall: it was built two summers ago from shipping boxes and painted midnight blue, with a cardboard tube for a telescope and a lens of polished glass. It creaks when the wind moves it and smells of dust and pencil marks where [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has labeled the stars. No one has taken it down.

- **The Stone Collection** — Kept in a jar by [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bedroom window: smooth stones from beaches and riverbeds, each chosen for its shape or color or the way light moves through it. There are forty-three of them. He knows each one's story.

- **Captain Crunch** — The fossil found on the beach at Cadaques two summers ago, the size of a child's hand, shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor depending on the light. It sits on the shelf above [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s desk, next to a drawing he made of what creature it might have been.

- **The Hill** — Rising behind the house, steep enough to demand respect, covered in low pine, wild thyme, and stones that roll underfoot. The path up it is used by shepherds but no one speaks about what is on the other side. The hill is old in a way the house is not.

- **The Village** — Houses clustered around a small plaza with a fountain, a baker, a bar where men drink coffee and argue, a schoolroom. It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a cardboard observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

## Rules

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R3.** The cardboard observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

## The feel of it

This book lives in the hours when a ten-year-old is most himself: curious, honest, stubborn, afraid of the dark but pretending not to be. The warmth is in the details—the shape of a stone, the way a dog sleeps, an old man who remembers things. The funny is small and true: a cardboard box painted blue, a fossil named after breakfast cereal, the way a child's logic works when an adult is listening. The fear is real and not dismissed—the dark is genuinely frightening, and bravery means going forward anyway—but it is held by the warmth of the dog at his side and the grandfather's voice in memory. This is a book about being on the edge of something larger than yourself, and choosing to step forward.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] · Bruno · Marcos · Rosa · Elena

### [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] — the protagonist, ten years old; curious, observant, brave though he denies his fear
Wants: to discover what lies on the other side of the hill and to be certain he is brave enough to go alone.
Wrong about: how invisible his fear is to the people who love him; they see him clearly.
Speaks: Direct and honest, with a habit of asking questions rather than making statements. When frightened, he hesitates and changes the subject. His voice is steady until it isn't.
Habit: Turns smooth stones over in his palms when thinking or anxious, reading their shape by touch as much as by sight.

### Bruno — scruffy terrier, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s constant companion; loyal, sensible, afraid of deep shadow but braver than he pretends
Wants: to follow [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and keep him safe, and to sleep warm at the foot of his bed.
Wrong about: Nothing much. His instincts about danger are correct.
Speaks: Through body language—whines sharply when frightened, circles before settling, stands close when anxious. His bark is quick and sharp when happy or alert.
Habit: Sleeps at the foot of [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bed every night, and circles three times before lying down anywhere.

### Marcos — the grandfather; patient, knowing, a builder of cardboard observatories; he walks slowly and speaks in stories
Wants: For [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers rather than be given them; to see the boy become himself.
Wrong about: That silence and stories alone are enough; sometimes a ten-year-old needs a direct answer.
Speaks: In circles and stories, often answering a question with another question. His voice is quiet and requires listening closely. He pauses for a long time before speaking, as if weighing words.
Habit: Pauses before answering, and taps his walking stick twice against the ground when about to tell the truth.

### Rosa — the baker's daughter, same age as [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]; practical, quick-thinking, braver than he is about admitting what frightens her
Wants: An adventure beyond the bakery and the village square; a friend who understands wanting to know what's beyond.
Wrong about: That [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] wants to do this alone; she does not ask, but she is meant to help.
Speaks: Quickly and directly, with humor and jokes when uncertain. Her words tumble out, and she laughs at her own nervous rambling. Flour dust marks her wherever she goes.
Habit: Brushes flour from her sleeves and apron without noticing she is doing it, a leftover from mornings in her mother's kitchen.

### Elena — a girl, twelve years old, living with her grandmother on the other side of the hill; quiet, observant, rooted to the land
Wants: To understand who climbs the hill and why; to know if anyone else collects the small treasures the earth gives up.
Wrong about: That the other side of the hill is as mysterious to others as her own life is to the village below.
Speaks: Carefully and slowly, as if testing each word. She asks simple questions that reach deeper than expected. Her voice is smaller than a ten-year-old's but steady.
Habit: Picks up small objects—pebbles, seeds, shells, anything the hill or the wind has left—and examines them closely, turning them over in her hands as if reading their stories.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

That evening, after supper had cleared and the light was turning long and gold across the garden, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found his father in the kitchen, moving slowly the way people do in heat, and asked him the question he had been holding since breakfast.

"Can I climb the hill again? Soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father looked at him for a long moment, and then smiled. "Yes," he said. "The same rule. And you'll follow it?"

"I will," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said, and he meant it the way he meant it on the day he first asked.

He was outside on the back path, heading toward the garden wall, when Rosa found him at the gate. She must have been waiting there, flour still in the creases of her sleeves, her hair coming loose from where she had pinned it that morning.

"There you are," she said, and her words tumbled out all at once. "I've been waiting since my mother let me go—I told her you'd be home by now, you had to be home by now, or she would have sent someone to look. What happened? What did you find? Did you see something? Is it as strange as everyone says, or is it just rocks and nothing? Tell me everything, you promised you would tell me everything."

She laughed at herself, embarrassed, and brushed flour from her sleeves without noticing she was doing it.

So he told her. About the path that got harder to see. About Bruno pressed against his leg, whining. About reaching the crest and seeing the valley spread out below like a secret the hill had been keeping. About Elena, who was twelve and had a house there with her grandmother, and a fossil of her own—pale and spiral-shaped—sitting on a shelf like Captain Crunch sat on his. About how the sun touched the horizon and he had to stop, so he stayed, and the dark was not the thing he had been afraid of after all. About waking early and climbing down in the grey light, Elena steady beside him and Bruno between them.

Rosa's eyes grew wider with each thing he said.

"You stayed there all night?" she asked.

"Yes."

"And you came back the next morning?"

"Yes."

"And Elena—is she kind?"

"Yes," he said. "She collects things the earth leaves behind. Like I do."

Rosa nodded slowly, turning this over in her mind the way she turned flour between her fingers. Then she said, "Next time you go, can I come?"

"Yes," he said, and knew his father would say yes too.

He found Marcos in the kitchen, moving slowly, the way the grandfather moved through almost everything. The old man looked at him without speaking for a moment, and then tapped his walking stick twice against the ground, the sound it made dry and certain.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] took a breath.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud.

Marcos tapped his stick twice. And then he spoke plainly, in one sentence, the way people speak who have decided that a young person has earned the truth:

"Yes—she will want to see what you have made of the light."

No story circled around the answer. No question answered with a question. The old man had simply said what he meant, and the weight of that directness was heavier and kinder than any story could have been.

Together, they walked out into the garden as the evening began to change color, Marcos moving slowly with his stick, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] keeping pace beside him. The cardboard observatory stood where it always stood, near the back wall, midnight blue and creaking faintly in the warm breeze. Up close, you could see all the places where the boxes had been taped together, where seams showed underneath the paint like old scars. The pencil marks where eight-year-old [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had drawn the stars were still there—some in the right places, some not quite, some doubling back on themselves because he had not been sure.

Marcos opened the door, and they went inside.

It smelled like it always smelled: dust and pencil shavings and something like the memory of cardboard. The polished glass lens caught the last of the sun and threw it across the small interior, and the cardboard tube that had been meant for a telescope stood waiting, patient and crooked in a way that made it look kind.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed onto the low shelf and Marcos handed him Captain Crunch—the fossil he had found two summers ago at Cadaques, shaped like a sleeping thing, smooth from the sea. The boy placed it on the highest shelf where the light would catch it, there where the best of the evening sun fell.

Then he climbed down and brought the jar of stones from where he kept it, and one by one he and Marcos arranged them on the shelf beside the fossil. The striped grey stone he had left for Elena glowed where it caught the light. The smooth river stones sorted themselves by color: white and rust and amber. The black stone from the beach caught the sun and held it like a secret.

Marcos stood quiet, looking at what they had made.

Outside the open door, Bruno had circled three times in the dust of the garden path and was now asleep, his chin resting on his paws, the warmth of the day still in his fur. The cicadas had begun their evening song. The sky above the garden was turning that particular blue that comes just before dusk, the blue that holds gold around its edges.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] stood beside his grandfather, and together they looked at the light on the fossil and the stones, the way it moved across the shell-shape of Captain Crunch, the way the grey stone held the warmth of the last sun. Somewhere, on the other side of the hill, Elena was probably looking at the same sky.

The stars were beginning to appear, faint and patient, waiting for the last of the light to leave.

Marcos did not speak. Neither did the boy. There was nothing that needed saying.

Outside, the evening deepened, and the garden held them both.

GENRE AND TONE:
a warm, funny children's adventure — a read-aloud summer quest told close to the ground, brave and kind; small real wonders rather than magic, a dog who is a character, and a fear of the dark taken seriously and gently.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] (the boy, ten years old — this literal bracketed token IS his name in this manuscript; write it exactly as `[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]`, every time, never substitute a real name)
Bruno (the terrier) · Marcos (the grandfather) · Rosa (the baker's daughter) · Elena (the girl on the other side, twelve) · Clara (Elena's grandmother) · Captain Crunch (the fossil)

# The World of The Other Side of the Hill

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] lives in a house at the edge of a small village in a landscape of stone and scrub, where the Mediterranean heat eases in the evening and the cicadas know when to start their song. The house is old enough to have stories but young enough to still live in them. Behind it rises a hill that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has never crossed, though he has stood at its foot a hundred times and wondered what a person might find there. This summer, the summer he turns ten, he is old enough—or brave enough, or curious enough—to go and see. His scruffy terrier Bruno will come with him. His fossil, his stones, his grandfather's cardboard observatory, and the dark that waits when the sun goes down: all of these are part of the story of that crossing.

## Places

- **The House and Garden** — A stone house with a wide kitchen where the family gathers. The garden is dry and full of olive trees, wild rosemary, and the long shadow the house casts on summer afternoons. The cardboard observatory stands near the back wall: it was built two summers ago from shipping boxes and painted midnight blue, with a cardboard tube for a telescope and a lens of polished glass. It creaks when the wind moves it and smells of dust and pencil marks where [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has labeled the stars. No one has taken it down.

- **The Stone Collection** — Kept in a jar by [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bedroom window: smooth stones from beaches and riverbeds, each chosen for its shape or color or the way light moves through it. There are forty-three of them. He knows each one's story.

- **Captain Crunch** — The fossil found on the beach at Cadaques two summers ago, the size of a child's hand, shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor depending on the light. It sits on the shelf above [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s desk, next to a drawing he made of what creature it might have been.

- **The Hill** — Rising behind the house, steep enough to demand respect, covered in low pine, wild thyme, and stones that roll underfoot. The path up it is used by shepherds but no one speaks about what is on the other side. The hill is old in a way the house is not.

- **The Village** — Houses clustered around a small plaza with a fountain, a baker, a bar where men drink coffee and argue, a schoolroom. It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a cardboard observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

## Rules

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R3.** The cardboard observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

## The feel of it

This book lives in the hours when a ten-year-old is most himself: curious, honest, stubborn, afraid of the dark but pretending not to be. The warmth is in the details—the shape of a stone, the way a dog sleeps, an old man who remembers things. The funny is small and true: a cardboard box painted blue, a fossil named after breakfast cereal, the way a child's logic works when an adult is listening. The fear is real and not dismissed—the dark is genuinely frightening, and bravery means going forward anyway—but it is held by the warmth of the dog at his side and the grandfather's voice in memory. This is a book about being on the edge of something larger than yourself, and choosing to step forward.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

That evening, after supper had cleared and the light was turning long and gold across the garden, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found his father in the kitchen, moving slowly the way people do in heat, and asked him the question he had been holding since breakfast.

"Can I climb the hill again? Soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father looked at him for a long moment, and then smiled. "Yes," he said. "The same rule. And you'll follow it?"

"I will," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said, and he meant it the way he meant it on the day he first asked.

He was outside on the back path, heading toward the garden wall, when Rosa found him at the gate. She must have been waiting there, flour still in the creases of her sleeves, her hair coming loose from where she had pinned it that morning.

"There you are," she said, and her words tumbled out all at once. "I've been waiting since my mother let me go—I told her you'd be home by now, you had to be home by now, or she would have sent someone to look. What happened? What did you find? Did you see something? Is it as strange as everyone says, or is it just rocks and nothing? Tell me everything, you promised you would tell me everything."

She laughed at herself, embarrassed, and brushed flour from her sleeves without noticing she was doing it.

So he told her. About the path that got harder to see. About Bruno pressed against his leg, whining. About reaching the crest and seeing the valley spread out below like a secret the hill had been keeping. About Elena, who was twelve and had a house there with her grandmother, and a fossil of her own—pale and spiral-shaped—sitting on a shelf like Captain Crunch sat on his. About how the sun touched the horizon and he had to stop, so he stayed, and the dark was not the thing he had been afraid of after all. About waking early and climbing down in the grey light, Elena steady beside him and Bruno between them.

Rosa's eyes grew wider with each thing he said.

"You stayed there all night?" she asked.

"Yes."

"And you came back the next morning?"

"Yes."

"And Elena—is she kind?"

"Yes," he said. "She collects things the earth leaves behind. Like I do."

Rosa nodded slowly, turning this over in her mind the way she turned flour between her fingers. Then she said, "Next time you go, can I come?"

"Yes," he said, and knew his father would say yes too.

He found Marcos in the kitchen, moving slowly, the way the grandfather moved through almost everything. The old man looked at him without speaking for a moment, and then tapped his walking stick twice against the ground, the sound it made dry and certain.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] took a breath.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud.

Marcos tapped his stick twice. And then he spoke plainly, in one sentence, the way people speak who have decided that a young person has earned the truth:

"Yes—she will want to see what you have made of the light."

No story circled around the answer. No question answered with a question. The old man had simply said what he meant, and the weight of that directness was heavier and kinder than any story could have been.

Together, they walked out into the garden as the evening began to change color, Marcos moving slowly with his stick, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] keeping pace beside him. The cardboard observatory stood where it always stood, near the back wall, midnight blue and creaking faintly in the warm breeze. Up close, you could see all the places where the boxes had been taped together, where seams showed underneath the paint like old scars. The pencil marks where eight-year-old [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had drawn the stars were still there—some in the right places, some not quite, some doubling back on themselves because he had not been sure.

Marcos opened the door, and they went inside.

It smelled like it always smelled: dust and pencil shavings and something like the memory of cardboard. The polished glass lens caught the last of the sun and threw it across the small interior, and the cardboard tube that had been meant for a telescope stood waiting, patient and crooked in a way that made it look kind.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed onto the low shelf and Marcos handed him Captain Crunch—the fossil he had found two summers ago at Cadaques, shaped like a sleeping thing, smooth from the sea. The boy placed it on the highest shelf where the light would catch it, there where the best of the evening sun fell.

Then he climbed down and brought the jar of stones from where he kept it, and one by one he and Marcos arranged them on the shelf beside the fossil. The striped grey stone he had left for Elena glowed where it caught the light. The smooth river stones sorted themselves by color: white and rust and amber. The black stone from the beach caught the sun and held it like a secret.

Marcos stood quiet, looking at what they had made.

Outside the open door, Bruno had circled three times in the dust of the garden path and was now asleep, his chin resting on his paws, the warmth of the day still in his fur. The cicadas had begun their evening song. The sky above the garden was turning that particular blue that comes just before dusk, the blue that holds gold around its edges.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] stood beside his grandfather, and together they looked at the light on the fossil and the stones, the way it moved across the shell-shape of Captain Crunch, the way the grey stone held the warmth of the last sun. Somewhere, on the other side of the hill, Elena was probably looking at the same sky.

The stars were beginning to appear, faint and patient, waiting for the last of the light to leave.

Marcos did not speak. Neither did the boy. There was nothing that needed saying.

Outside, the evening deepened, and the garden held them both.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

That evening, after supper had cleared and the light was turning long and gold across the garden, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found his father in the kitchen, moving slowly the way people do in heat, and asked him the question he had been holding since breakfast.

"Can I climb the hill again? Soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father looked at him for a long moment, and then smiled. "Yes," he said. "The same rule. And you'll follow it?"

"I will," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said, and he meant it the way he meant it on the day he first asked.

He was outside on the back path, heading toward the garden wall, when Rosa found him at the gate. She must have been waiting there, flour still in the creases of her sleeves, her hair coming loose from where she had pinned it that morning.

"There you are," she said, and her words tumbled out all at once. "I've been waiting since my mother let me go—I told her you'd be home by now, you had to be home by now, or she would have sent someone to look. What happened? What did you find? Did you see something? Is it as strange as everyone says, or is it just rocks and nothing? Tell me everything, you promised you would tell me everything."

She laughed at herself, embarrassed, and brushed flour from her sleeves without noticing she was doing it.

So he told her. About the path that got harder to see. About Bruno pressed against his leg, whining. About reaching the crest and seeing the valley spread out below like a secret the hill had been keeping. About Elena, who was twelve and had a house there with her grandmother, and a fossil of her own—pale and spiral-shaped—sitting on a shelf like Captain Crunch sat on his. About how the sun touched the horizon and he had to stop, so he stayed, and the dark was not the thing he had been afraid of after all. About waking early and climbing down in the grey light, Elena steady beside him and Bruno between them.

Rosa's eyes grew wider with each thing he said.

"You stayed there all night?" she asked.

"Yes."

"And you came back the next morning?"

"Yes."

"And Elena—is she kind?"

"Yes," he said. "She collects things the earth leaves behind. Like I do."

Rosa nodded slowly, turning this over in her mind the way she turned flour between her fingers. Then she said, "Next time you go, can I come?"

"Yes," he said, and knew his father would say yes too.

He found Marcos in the kitchen, moving slowly, the way the grandfather moved through almost everything. The old man looked at him without speaking for a moment, and then tapped his walking stick twice against the ground, the sound it made dry and certain.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] took a breath.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud.

Marcos tapped his stick twice. And then he spoke plainly, in one sentence, the way people speak who have decided that a young person has earned the truth:

"Yes—she will want to see what you have made of the light."

No story circled around the answer. No question answered with a question. The old man had simply said what he meant, and the weight of that directness was heavier and kinder than any story could have been.

Together, they walked out into the garden as the evening began to change color, Marcos moving slowly with his stick, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] keeping pace beside him. The cardboard observatory stood where it always stood, near the back wall, midnight blue and creaking faintly in the warm breeze. Up close, you could see all the places where the boxes had been taped together, where seams showed underneath the paint like old scars. The pencil marks where eight-year-old [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had drawn the stars were still there—some in the right places, some not quite, some doubling back on themselves because he had not been sure.

Marcos opened the door, and they went inside.

It smelled like it always smelled: dust and pencil shavings and something like the memory of cardboard. The polished glass lens caught the last of the sun and threw it across the small interior, and the cardboard tube that had been meant for a telescope stood waiting, patient and crooked in a way that made it look kind.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed onto the low shelf and Marcos handed him Captain Crunch—the fossil he had found two summers ago at Cadaques, shaped like a sleeping thing, smooth from the sea. The boy placed it on the highest shelf where the light would catch it, there where the best of the evening sun fell.

Then he climbed down and brought the jar of stones from where he kept it, and one by one he and Marcos arranged them on the shelf beside the fossil. The striped grey stone he had left for Elena glowed where it caught the light. The smooth river stones sorted themselves by color: white and rust and amber. The black stone from the beach caught the sun and held it like a secret.

Marcos stood quiet, looking at what they had made.

Outside the open door, Bruno had circled three times in the dust of the garden path and was now asleep, his chin resting on his paws, the warmth of the day still in his fur. The cicadas had begun their evening song. The sky above the garden was turning that particular blue that comes just before dusk, the blue that holds gold around its edges.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] stood beside his grandfather, and together they looked at the light on the fossil and the stones, the way it moved across the shell-shape of Captain Crunch, the way the grey stone held the warmth of the last sun. Somewhere, on the other side of the hill, Elena was probably looking at the same sky.

The stars were beginning to appear, faint and patient, waiting for the last of the light to leave.

Marcos did not speak. Neither did the boy. There was nothing that needed saying.

Outside, the evening deepened, and the garden held them both.

"You stayed there all night?" she asked.

"Yes."

"And you came back the next morning?"

"Yes."

"And Elena—is she kind?"

"Yes," he said. "She collects things the earth leaves behind. Like I do."

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

That evening, after supper had cleared and the light was turning long and gold across the garden, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found his father in the kitchen, moving slowly the way people do in heat, and asked him the question he had been holding since breakfast.

"Can I climb the hill again? Soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father looked at him for a long moment, and then smiled. "Yes," he said. "The same rule. And you'll follow it?"

"I will," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said, and he meant it the way he meant it on the day he first asked.

He was outside on the back path, heading toward the garden wall, when Rosa found him at the gate. She must have been waiting there, flour still in the creases of her sleeves, her hair coming loose from where she had pinned it that morning.

"There you are," she said, and her words tumbled out all at once. "I've been waiting since my mother let me go—I told her you'd be home by now, you had to be home by now, or she would have sent someone to look. What happened? What did you find? Did you see something? Is it as strange as everyone says, or is it just rocks and nothing? Tell me everything, you promised you would tell me everything."

She laughed at herself, embarrassed, and brushed flour from her sleeves without noticing she was doing it.

So he told her. About the path that got harder to see. About Bruno pressed against his leg, whining. About reaching the crest and seeing the valley spread out below like a secret the hill had been keeping. About Elena, who was twelve and had a house there with her grandmother, and a fossil of her own—pale and spiral-shaped—sitting on a shelf like Captain Crunch sat on his. About how the sun touched the horizon and he had to stop, so he stayed, and the dark was not the thing he had been afraid of after all. About waking early and climbing down in the grey light, Elena steady beside him and Bruno between them.

Rosa's eyes grew wider with each thing he said.

"You stayed there all night?" she asked.

"Yes."

"And you came back the next morning?"

"Yes."

"And Elena—is she kind?"

"Yes," he said. "She collects things the earth leaves behind. Like I do."

Rosa nodded slowly, turning this over in her mind the way she turned flour between her fingers. Then she said, "Next time you go, can I come?"

"Yes," he said, and knew his father would say yes too.

He found Marcos in the kitchen, moving slowly, the way the grandfather moved through almost everything. The old man looked at him without speaking for a moment, and then tapped his walking stick twice against the ground, the sound it made dry and certain.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] took a breath.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud.

Marcos tapped his stick twice. And then he spoke plainly, in one sentence, the way people speak who have decided that a young person has earned the truth:

"Yes—she will want to see what you have made of the light."

No story circled around the answer. No question answered with a question. The old man had simply said what he meant, and the weight of that directness was heavier and kinder than any story could have been.

Together, they walked out into the garden as the evening began to change color, Marcos moving slowly with his stick, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] keeping pace beside him. The cardboard observatory stood where it always stood, near the back wall, midnight blue and creaking faintly in the warm breeze. Up close, you could see all the places where the boxes had been taped together, where seams showed underneath the paint like old scars. The pencil marks where eight-year-old [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had drawn the stars were still there—some in the right places, some not quite, some doubling back on themselves because he had not been sure.

Marcos opened the door, and they went inside.

It smelled like it always smelled: dust and pencil shavings and something like the memory of cardboard. The polished glass lens caught the last of the sun and threw it across the small interior, and the cardboard tube that had been meant for a telescope stood waiting, patient and crooked in a way that made it look kind.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed onto the low shelf and Marcos handed him Captain Crunch—the fossil he had found two summers ago at Cadaques, shaped like a sleeping thing, smooth from the sea. The boy placed it on the highest shelf where the light would catch it, there where the best of the evening sun fell.

Then he climbed down and brought the jar of stones from where he kept it, and one by one he and Marcos arranged them on the shelf beside the fossil. The striped grey stone he had left for Elena glowed where it caught the light. The smooth river stones sorted themselves by color: white and rust and amber. The black stone from the beach caught the sun and held it like a secret.

Marcos stood quiet, looking at what they had made.

Outside the open door, Bruno had circled three times in the dust of the garden path and was now asleep, his chin resting on his paws, the warmth of the day still in his fur. The cicadas had begun their evening song. The sky above the garden was turning that particular blue that comes just before dusk, the blue that holds gold around its edges.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] stood beside his grandfather, and together they looked at the light on the fossil and the stones, the way it moved across the shell-shape of Captain Crunch, the way the grey stone held the warmth of the last sun. Somewhere, on the other side of the hill, Elena was probably looking at the same sky.

The stars were beginning to appear, faint and patient, waiting for the last of the light to leave.

Marcos did not speak. Neither did the boy. There was nothing that needed saying.

Outside, the evening deepened, and the garden held them both.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

That evening, after supper had cleared and the light was turning long and gold across the garden, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found his father in the kitchen, moving slowly the way people do in heat, and asked him the question he had been holding since breakfast.

"Can I climb the hill again? Soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father looked at him for a long moment, and then smiled. "Yes," he said. "The same rule. And you'll follow it?"

"I will," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said, and he meant it the way he had on the day he first asked.

He was outside on the back path, heading toward the garden wall, when Rosa found him at the gate. She must have been waiting there, flour still in the creases of her sleeves, her hair coming loose from where she had pinned it that morning.

"There you are," she said, and her words tumbled out all at once. "I've been waiting since my mother let me go—I told her you'd be home by now, you had to be home by now, or she would have sent someone to look. What happened? What did you find? Did you see something? Is it as strange as everyone says, or is it just rocks and nothing? Tell me everything, you promised you would tell me everything."

She laughed at herself, embarrassed, and brushed flour from her sleeves without noticing she was doing it.

So he told her. About the path that got harder to see. About Bruno pressed against his leg, whining. About the thyme that rose in a smell when you trod on it, and the quick grey birds calling from places you couldn't locate. About how steep it was, steeper than it looked from below. About reaching the crest and seeing the valley spread out below like a secret the hill had been keeping. About Elena, who was twelve and had a house there with her grandmother, and a fossil of her own—pale and spiral-shaped—sitting on a shelf like Captain Crunch sat on his. About how the sun touched the horizon and he had to stop, so he stayed, and the dark was not the thing he had been afraid of after all. About waking early and climbing down in the grey light, Elena steady beside him and Bruno between them.

Rosa's eyes grew wider with each thing he said.

"You stayed there all night?" she asked.

"Yes."

"And you came back the next morning?"

"Yes."

"And Elena—is she kind?"

"Yes," he said. "She collects things the earth leaves behind. Like I do."

Rosa nodded slowly, turning this over in her mind the way she turned flour between her fingers. Then she said, "Next time you go, can I come?"

"Yes," he said, and knew his father would say yes too.

He found Marcos in the kitchen, moving slowly, the way the grandfather moved through almost everything. The old man looked at him without speaking for a long moment.

He could see it already—Elena standing in the doorway of the cardboard box, looking up at the painted stars. But it wasn't only his to show her. It was half Marcos's. He took a breath.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud.

Marcos tapped his stick twice. And then he spoke plainly, in one sentence, the way people speak who have decided that a young person has earned the truth:

"Yes—she will want to see what you have made of the light."

Together, they walked out into the garden as the evening began to change color, Marcos moving slowly with his stick, and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] keeping pace beside him. The cardboard observatory stood where it always stood, near the back wall, midnight blue and creaking faintly in the warm breeze. Up close, you could see all the places where the boxes had been taped together, where seams showed underneath the paint like old scars. The pencil marks where eight-year-old [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had drawn the stars were still there—some in the right places, some not quite, some doubling back on themselves because he had not been sure.

Marcos opened the door, and they went inside.

It smelled like it always smelled: dust and pencil shavings and something like the memory of cardboard. The polished glass lens caught the last of the sun and threw it across the small interior, and the cardboard tube that had been meant for a telescope stood waiting, patient and crooked in a way that made it look kind.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed onto the low shelf and Marcos handed him Captain Crunch—the fossil he had found two summers ago at Cadaques, shaped like a sleeping thing, smooth from the sea. The boy placed it on the highest shelf where the light would catch it, there where the best of the evening sun fell.

Then he climbed down and brought the jar of stones from where he kept it, and one by one he and Marcos arranged them on the shelf beside the fossil. The amber river stone glowed where it caught the light. The smooth river stones sorted themselves by color: white and rust and amber. The black stone from the beach caught the sun and held it like a secret.

Marcos stood quiet, looking at what they had made.

Outside the open door, Bruno had circled three times in the dust of the garden path and was now asleep, his chin resting on his paws, the warmth of the day still in his fur. The cicadas had begun their evening song. The sky above the garden was turning that particular blue that comes just before dusk, the blue that holds gold around its edges.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] stood beside his grandfather, and together they looked at the light on the fossil and the stones, the way it moved across the shell-shape of Captain Crunch, the way the amber stone held the warmth of the last sun. Somewhere, on the other side of the hill, Elena was probably looking at the same sky.

The stars were beginning to appear, faint and patient, waiting for the last of the light to leave.

Marcos did not speak. Neither did the boy. There was nothing that needed saying.

Outside, the evening deepened, and the garden held them both.

input.content:
Day 5, evening. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found his father in the kitchen and asked whether he could climb the hill again soon, with the same rule — home before dark. His father said yes, and asked whether he would follow it, and he said he would.

Rosa was at the gate, and had been waiting. Her words came out all at once, and she reminded him he had promised to tell her everything. So he told her: the path that got harder to see, Bruno pressed against his leg and whining, the thyme that rose in a smell when you trod on it, the quick grey birds calling from places you could not locate, how much steeper it was than it looks from below, the valley, Elena, her fossil, the night, the walk down at dawn. Rosa asked whether Elena was kind. Then she asked whether she could come next time, and he said yes.

He went in to Marcos. He could see it already — Elena standing in the doorway of the cardboard observatory, looking up at the painted stars — and then the fact arrived that it was not only his to show. He asked aloud: can I show Elena the observatory? Marcos tapped his stick twice and answered plainly, in one sentence: yes, she will want to see what he has made of the light.

They went out together. Inside the observatory they put Captain Crunch on the high shelf where the light falls and arranged the smooth stones beside it. Bruno slept in the dust through the open door. The stars came out.

content.content:
1	# Chapter 1 — Ten Years Old
2	
3	[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] woke before the cicadas stopped singing. The light through his window was already the color of honey, which meant it was late enough that the kitchen would be warm and his grandmother might have left honey on the table with the bread. He lay still for a moment, listening to the particular quiet of ten-year-old mornings — the kind of quiet that felt like it was waiting for something.
4	
5	Bruno lifted his head from the foot of the bed, saw that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was awake, and remembered that he had been sleeping there without permission again. The small terrier scrambled into a tighter ball, but his tail kept moving, betraying him.
6	
7	"You can stay," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said.
8	
9	The kitchen was exactly as he'd pictured: honey on the table, bread still warm in its cloth, his mother already wearing the look she got on birthday mornings — the one that meant she had been awake for hours. His father was reading the newspaper but reading slowly, the kind of reading that meant he was waiting to look up at something.
10	
11	"Ten," his father said, not looking away from the page. "Today you are ten."
12	
13	Marcos arrived while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was still eating. His grandfather moved through the door the way he moved through everything, as though he had already walked this path a hundred times and knew exactly where every stone was. He carried a small package wrapped in brown paper, the kind of brown paper that looked like it had been chosen carefully rather than torn from whatever was nearest.
14	
15	"The stones told me you were ready," Marcos said, which was what Marcos said about most things. He set the package on the table.
16	
17	Inside was a notebook. Not a school notebook with lines that ruled your thinking into neat rows, but a leather-bound book with blank pages and a spine that creaked when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] opened it. The leather was soft and darker on the edges where it had been handled, as though the book had been someone else's for a long time before becoming his.
18	
19	"For seeing," Marcos said. He tapped his walking stick twice against the stone floor. "Not writing down the answers. Writing down the questions you couldn't ask anyone else."
20	
21	[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] turned the first page slowly. It was empty and it felt important, like standing at the edge of something.
22	
23	"There's a pencil," his mother said. "In the kitchen drawer. The sharp one we keep."
24	
25	Bruno followed him to his room. The dog always followed him to his room, but today it felt intentional, as though Bruno understood that something had shifted in the house. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] opened the window wider to let more light in, then climbed onto his chair to reach the shelf above his desk.
26	
27	Captain Crunch sat where he always sat, fossil-hard and ancient and worn smooth by whatever water or time had touched it before [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] found it two summers ago on the beach at Cadaques. His father had laughed when he named it after the cereal with the cartoon pirate on the box, and then everyone had laughed, and then nobody had called it anything else. It was not a formal name, but it was the real one.
28	
29	He placed the new notebook carefully beside the fossil, close enough that they looked as though they belonged together. The afternoon light coming through the window was different from the light he usually saw at this hour, or maybe the leather of the notebook was catching it and throwing it back in a way that made everything look sharper. He picked up Captain Crunch — the familiar weight of it, the smooth curve that felt like it had been made to fit his palm — and looked at it in this new brightness.
30	
31	The light showed him something he hadn't quite seen before: a thin ridge that ran along one side, like the edge of a shell, like something that had once been alive and had folded itself into this shape. He turned it slowly. Maybe it had been a creature that curled up when it was afraid. He set it down gently and opened the notebook.
32	
33	With the sharp pencil, he wrote the first question: "What shape was it?"
34	
35	He did not write the answer. Marcos had been clear about that.
36	
37	Bruno had found the cool corner of the room where the stone wall stayed cold even when the rest of the house burned with summer heat. He circled three times and collapsed onto the rough tile, his chin resting on his paws, watching [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] with the patient expression of a dog who knew there would be supper eventually.
38	
39	At the kitchen table at six o'clock exactly, when the light had turned golden and starting to lean toward evening, his mother set the bread down and his father folded his newspaper. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s mother had made the soup that meant something was being celebrated, the one with tomatoes and basil and small pasta shapes, the one that took all morning.
40	
41	"Your mother wants to know if you're planning to do something dangerous with your birthday," his father said.
42	
43	"I'm ten," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said. "I'm not afraid of anything."
44	
45	His father waited, the way adults do when they know you haven't finished speaking.
46	
47	"I want to go to the hill," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said.
48	
49	The spoon stopped in his mother's hand. Not for long — she was watching him carefully but not as though he'd said something impossible. Marcos, who had appeared at the table as he always did at supper time, looked at his own bowl.
50	
51	"You're old enough," his father said. He cut his bread in half. "You'll go in the daylight. You'll be home before the sun touches the horizon. That is the only rule about the hill."
52	
53	"The sun touches—" [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] started.
54	
55	"When it is fully down," his father said, "the paths change. Distance becomes unreliable. You don't go learning a place in the dark." He put the bread in his mouth and chewed. His father was not a person who gave long speeches. When he spoke, it meant something. "When you are older and you've crossed it a hundred times in daylight, then you can think about learning it in the dark. For now: daylight. Home before the sun touches the horizon."
56	
57	Bruno ate steadily from his own bowl under the table, an arrangement nobody had officially agreed to but everyone had understood for years. His tail thumped the floor in the rhythm of a dog who knew that supper meant eventually [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] would also be under the table, dropping pieces of bread.
58	
59	[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] didn't answer. The rule was clear. The rule wasn't unreasonable — it was just that suddenly the hill was real in a way it hadn't been before, and real things that are allowed are somehow much more frightening than things that are forbidden.
60	
61	He reached into his pocket where, without deciding to, he had put one of the stones from his collection that morning. It was a small smooth stone from the river, gray with a white stripe running through it, the kind that fit perfectly in the hollow of his palm. He turned it over and over while he ate, feeling its warmth under the kitchen light, while his father folded his newspaper again, and his mother watched him with the look that said she knew this day had meant something, and the stone turned, and turned, in his hands.
62

Bruno lifted his head from the foot of the bed, saw that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was awake, and remembered that he had been sleeping there without permission again. The small terrier scrambled into a tighter ball, but his tail kept moving, betraying him.

His father was reading the newspaper but reading slowly, the kind of reading that meant he was waiting to look up at something.

"Ten," his father said, not looking away from the page. "Today you are ten."

Marcos arrived while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] was still eating. His grandfather moved through the door the way he moved through everything, as though he had already walked this path a hundred times and knew exactly where every stone was. He carried a small package wrapped in brown paper, the kind of brown paper that looked like it had been chosen carefully rather than torn from whatever was nearest.

"The stones told me you were ready," Marcos said, which was what Marcos said about most things. He set the package on the table.

The leather was soft and darker on the edges where it had been handled, as though the book had been someone else's for a long time before becoming his.

His father had laughed when he named it after the cereal with the cartoon pirate on the box, and then everyone had laughed, and then nobody had called it anything else. It was not a formal name, but it was the real one.

He placed the new notebook carefully beside the fossil, close enough that they looked as though they belonged together. The afternoon light coming through the window was different from the light he usually saw at this hour, or maybe the leather of the notebook was catching it and throwing it back in a way that made everything look sharper. The light showed him something he hadn't quite seen before: a thin ridge that ran along one side, like the edge of a shell, like something that had once been alive and had folded itself into this shape. He turned it slowly. Maybe it had been a creature that curled up when it was afraid. He set it down gently and opened the notebook.

With the sharp pencil, he wrote the first question: "What shape was it?"

He did not write the answer. Marcos had been clear about that.

Bruno had found the cool corner of the room where the stone wall stayed cold even when the rest of the house burned with summer heat. He circled three times and collapsed onto the rough tile, his chin resting on his paws, watching [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] with the patient expression of a dog who knew there would be supper eventually.

At the kitchen table at six o'clock exactly, when the light had turned golden and starting to lean toward evening, his mother set the bread down and his father folded his newspaper. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s mother had made the soup that meant something was being celebrated, the one with tomatoes and basil and small pasta shapes, the one that took all morning.

"Your mother wants to know if you're planning to do something dangerous with your birthday," his father said.

"I'm ten," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said. "I'm not afraid of anything."

His father waited, the way adults do when they know you haven't finished speaking.

"I want to go to the hill," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said.

The spoon stopped in his mother's hand. Not for long — she was watching him carefully but not as though he'd said something impossible. Marcos, who had appeared at the table as he always did at supper time, looked at his own bowl.

"You're old enough," his father said. He cut his bread in half. "You'll go in the daylight. You'll be home before the sun touches the horizon. That is the only rule about the hill."

"The sun touches—" [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] started.

"When it is fully down," his father said, "the paths change. Distance becomes unreliable. You don't go learning a place in the dark." He put the bread in his mouth and chewed. His father was not a person who gave long speeches. When he spoke, it meant something. "When you are older and you've crossed it a hundred times in daylight, then you can think about learning it in the dark. For now: daylight. Home before the sun touches the horizon."

Bruno ate steadily from his own bowl under the table, an arrangement nobody had officially agreed to but everyone had understood for years. His tail thumped the floor in the rhythm of a dog who knew that supper meant eventually [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] would also be under the table, dropping pieces of bread.

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] didn't answer. The rule was clear. The rule wasn't unreasonable — it was just that suddenly the hill was real in a way it hadn't been before, and real things that are allowed are somehow much more frightening than things that are forbidden.

He reached into his pocket where, without deciding to, he had put one of the stones from his collection that morning. It was a small smooth stone from the river, gray with a white stripe running through it, the kind that fit perfectly in the hollow of his palm. He turned it over and over while he ate, feeling its warmth under the kitchen light, while his father folded his newspaper again, and his mother watched him with the look that said she knew this day had meant something, and the stone turned, and turned, in his hands.
